# Product Specification: Table booking and waitlist for Saltwick Dining Group

Version 0.9, owner: Beatrix Oduya, Product. Applies to the web booking widget and the host-stand tablet app at all 7 restaurants.

## 1. Overview

Guests can book a table online for 1 to 12 people. When no table is free at the requested time, they can join a waitlist for that date. Hosts manage the floor on a tablet. The system replaces the current phone-and-paper process.

## 2. Booking rules

2.1 A booking has a restaurant, a date, a time slot, a party size, a guest name, a mobile phone number and an optional note (maximum 200 characters).
2.2 Time slots are every 15 minutes between the restaurant's opening time and 90 minutes before closing. Each restaurant defines its own opening hours per weekday and may mark single dates as closed.
2.3 A booking can be made up to 60 days ahead and no later than 2 hours before the slot, except that hosts can add bookings at any time.
2.4 Standard dining duration is 90 minutes for parties of 1 to 4, 120 minutes for parties of 5 to 8 and 150 minutes for parties of 9 to 12. A table is blocked for the duration plus a 15-minute turnover buffer.
2.5 The system assigns a table automatically. It selects the smallest free table whose capacity is at least the party size and whose capacity is not more than the party size plus 2. Tables can be combined only if the restaurant has marked them as combinable, and only for parties of 7 or more.
2.6 Parties larger than 8 pay a deposit of 10 euros per person by card at booking time. The deposit is refunded in full if the booking is cancelled at least 24 hours before the slot, and is otherwise kept. The deposit is subtracted from the final bill by the host.
2.7 A guest may have at most 3 future bookings at one restaurant and at most 5 in total across all restaurants. The phone number identifies the guest.
2.8 Restaurants have a daily cap on the number of covers booked online (default 80% of seated capacity) so that walk-in guests can be served.

## 3. Confirmation and reminders

3.1 After booking, the guest receives an SMS within 1 minute with the details and a link to change or cancel.
3.2 24 hours before the slot, the guest receives a reminder SMS with a one-tap button to confirm or cancel. If a guest does not respond, the booking stays valid.
3.3 Guests can change the time or party size from the link until 2 hours before the slot. A change is treated as a new availability check; if the new request cannot be met, the old booking stays.
3.4 Cancellations free the table immediately. If a waitlist exists for that date, see section 4.

## 4. Waitlist

4.1 A guest may join a waitlist for a date, a party size and a time window (for example, 19:00 to 21:00). The waitlist is first come, first served.
4.2 When a table that fits becomes free inside a waiting guest's window, the system sends an SMS offering the slot. The guest has 15 minutes to accept by tapping the link. If the offer is not accepted in 15 minutes, it moves to the next guest.
4.3 If the freed slot is less than 3 hours away, the acceptance window is shortened to 8 minutes.
4.4 A guest can be on at most 2 waitlists for the same date.
4.5 When a guest accepts, the booking is created as in section 2 and the guest is removed from the waitlist. The deposit rule in 2.6 applies, and the offer payment must be made at acceptance.

## 5. Host app

5.1 The host sees a timeline of the floor by table, with bookings in colour: expected (blue), arrived (green), seated (grey), late by 15 minutes or more (amber), no-show (red).
5.2 A booking is marked as late automatically 15 minutes after the slot and as a no-show after 30 minutes, unless the host marks the guest as arrived. A no-show releases the table and its deposit is kept.
5.3 Hosts can create walk-in entries, move bookings between tables, override the table assignment, extend a seating by 15, 30 or 60 minutes, and block tables.
5.4 When a host moves a booking to a table that creates a conflict with another booking, the app warns and requires confirmation.
5.5 The host app works offline for up to 30 minutes and synchronises on reconnection. If two devices change the same booking while offline, the most recent change wins and the other device shows a notice.

## 6. Reporting and permissions

6.1 Managers can view a daily report: covers booked, covers seated, no-shows, cancellations, average party size, waitlist conversions.
6.2 There are three roles: host (floor and bookings), manager (host plus reports and opening hours) and group admin (manager for every restaurant plus user management).

## 6A. Payments and refunds

6A.1 Deposits are taken by card through the group's payment provider; card details never reach the booking system, which stores only a payment reference. 6A.2 If a payment fails, the booking is held for 10 minutes so the guest can try another card, and is then released. 6A.3 A refund under rule 2.6 is issued automatically when the guest cancels through the link at least 24 hours before the slot; the system sends an SMS to confirm. 6A.4 If a booking is changed so that the party size drops to 8 or fewer, the deposit is refunded in full. If the party size rises above 8, the additional deposit is requested at the time of change and the change is not applied until it is paid. 6A.5 Hosts can waive a deposit forfeiture for a no-show, with a reason, but only managers can approve a waiver over 100 euros.

## 6B. Special dates and closures

6B.1 A manager can close a restaurant for a date, in which case all existing bookings for that date are cancelled and the guests receive an SMS with a link to rebook at another restaurant of the group, and any deposits are refunded. 6B.2 On dates marked "special menu" (for example 24 December and 14 February), the slot interval is 30 minutes, the standard dining duration is 120 minutes for all party sizes, and a deposit of 15 euros per person applies to parties of 5 or more. 6B.3 A manager can set a maximum party size per restaurant, lower than 12, for example 8 at the smallest restaurant.

## 6C. Data retention

6C.1 Guest names and phone numbers are deleted 18 months after the last booking. 6C.2 A guest can ask to be deleted by replying STOP to any SMS; the system then removes the personal data within 24 hours, keeping an anonymised booking record for reporting. 6C.3 Guest notes are visible to hosts and managers only.

## 7. Non-functional requirements

7.1 The widget loads in less than 2 seconds on a mobile connection (4G). 7.2 The availability check takes less than 1 second at the 95th percentile. 7.3 The system supports 300 concurrent guests browsing. 7.4 Guest phone numbers are not shown to hosts until 24 hours before the booking time. 7.5 The widget works in English, French and Italian, and is accessible according to WCAG 2.1 level AA.

# RV Calder Sound: Cruise CS-26-07 Post-Cruise Report

Cruise dates: 14 September to 2 October 2026. Chief scientist: Dr. Imogen Faraday. Master: Captain Leif Haugland. Report prepared by the Marine Operations Office, 7 October 2026.

## 1. Purpose and summary

CS-26-07 was a 19-day cruise in the Skarra Basin to service three seabed moorings, collect water and sediment samples along a 240 km transect, and survey the habitat of a cold-water coral reef with the remotely operated vehicle (ROV) Tern. The vessel sailed from Alderport with 12 scientists, 3 technicians and 14 crew. Of 19 days, 15 were used at sea on science stations, 2 were spent in transit and 2 were lost to weather. All three moorings were recovered and redeployed, 61 of 64 planned water stations were completed and 8 of the 10 planned ROV dives were carried out. The budget was exceeded by 9.4%, mainly because of fuel and a repair to the ROV winch.

## 2. Operations

Departure was delayed by 14 hours because a hydraulic hose on the main crane had to be replaced. Weather was good from 14 to 22 September, with winds under 20 knots. From 23 to 24 September a low-pressure system brought winds of 40 to 45 knots and waves over 5 metres; no work was possible and the vessel took shelter in the lee of Skarra Island. Station work resumed on 25 September. The ship's dynamic positioning system worked well throughout, holding position within 3 metres during all ROV dives. The vessel returned to Alderport on 2 October at 06:40, 18 hours after the planned time because of the head wind.

## 3. Science results

**Moorings.** Mooring M1 was recovered with all instruments. Mooring M2 had lost its upper current meter, which had been fouled by fishing gear; the data stop on 11 January. Mooring M3 returned a full 14-month record. All three were redeployed with new batteries. **Water sampling.** The conductivity-temperature-depth (CTD) rosette was deployed 61 times. A fault in the water-bottle trigger in the first week affected 3 casts, which were repeated. 1,116 water samples were collected for nutrient and carbon analysis. **ROV.** Eight dives totalling 52 hours of bottom time were completed. Two dives were cancelled after the winch fault on 29 September. The survey covered 3.4 square kilometres of reef and recorded live coral colonies on 71% of the video transects. **Sediment.** 38 cores were taken; 5 had to be discarded because of disturbed layers.

## 4. Equipment and technical issues

The main crane hose failure on departure was the first of four equipment events. On 19 September the echosounder lost its signal for 6 hours and was reset by the electronics technician. On 29 September the ROV winch brake slipped during recovery of the vehicle and the tether was damaged; the vehicle itself was not hurt. The repair, using a spare slip ring and 140 metres of new cable, took 38 hours and cost 21,600 pounds. On 30 September the laboratory freezer failed overnight and the temperature rose to minus 9 degrees for about five hours. The scientific team judged that the samples inside were not affected, but this will be confirmed by the laboratory. The vessel's maintenance log records that the winch brake had been due for inspection in July.

## 5. Safety and health

There were no lost-time injuries. Two near-misses were reported: a wave struck the working deck on 23 September while a technician was securing a CTD frame; and a gas bottle was found to be unsecured on the lower deck. A scientist had to be treated for severe seasickness and recovered after two days. The crew conducted a fire drill and a man-overboard drill in the first week. Both were judged satisfactory, although the muster time for the second drill was 11 minutes, against a target of 8.

## 6. Environment

Fuel use was 412 tonnes, 7% above the plan, because of the weather and the extra transit. The vessel discharged no waste at sea except food waste, which was macerated and released more than 12 nautical miles from land. No spills occurred. The ROV did not touch the coral during any of its dives, according to the pilot's log.

## 7. Finance

The approved budget was 986,000 pounds. The actual cost was 1,078,700 pounds, an overspend of 92,700 pounds, or 9.4%. The overspend consisted of fuel (38,500 pounds), the winch repair (21,600 pounds), extra port and crew costs due to delays (19,200 pounds) and the cost of replacement instruments (13,400 pounds). These four items account for the whole overspend. The grant providers have been told that the overspend will be met from the operations reserve.

## 8. Crew and people

Feedback from the scientific party was positive about the ship's cabins and the cook. Several scientists said that the deck work briefing on the first day was too short, and that laboratory space was cramped when all 12 scientists were working. Two crew members left the vessel in Alderport, giving notice on health grounds. The chief engineer has asked for a spare winch brake assembly to be kept on board in future.

## 9. Data management and lessons learned

All CTD, mooring and echosounder data were copied to two portable drives and to the shore server by the end of the cruise; the ROV video (about 11 terabytes) was copied to the shore archive on 5 October and verified by checksum. The team's debrief identified four lessons. First, the weather window in late September is unreliable, and future cruises to the basin should carry two spare days. Second, the crane and winch inspections should be tied to the cruise calendar so that none falls due during a cruise. Third, the sample freezer needs a temperature alarm that reaches the bridge, because the failure was only discovered the next morning by a technician. Fourth, a second ROV pilot should be trained, because one pilot worked 11-hour days for the eight dives and the master considered this near the limit of safe fatigue.

## 10. Outstanding items

The freezer's repair estimate is awaited. The M2 mooring data gap needs a decision on whether to redeploy a second current meter at a cost of 17,000 pounds. The two cancelled ROV dives have to be rescheduled, ideally in the spring cruise. The operations board meets on 15 October.

Our theatre's ticketing database was designed in a hurry and the box office says that reports have become slow since the autumn season started. Please review the design, point out missing or useless indexes, and rewrite the five queries at the bottom with explanations of what was wrong with each version.

```sql
-- Schema for the Millbrook Repertory Theatre ticketing system (PostgreSQL)

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id   SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    full_name     TEXT NOT NULL,
    email         TEXT,
    phone         TEXT,
    postcode      TEXT,
    member_since  DATE,
    member_level  TEXT,           -- 'none', 'friend', 'patron'
    notes         TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE productions (
    production_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    title         TEXT NOT NULL,
    director      TEXT,
    season        TEXT,           -- e.g. 'Autumn 2026'
    base_price    NUMERIC(8,2)
);

CREATE TABLE performances (
    performance_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    production_id  INTEGER REFERENCES productions(production_id),
    starts_at      TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    venue          TEXT NOT NULL, -- 'main stage' or 'studio'
    capacity       INTEGER NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE seats (
    seat_id   SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    venue     TEXT NOT NULL,
    row_label TEXT NOT NULL,
    seat_no   INTEGER NOT NULL,
    zone      TEXT NOT NULL       -- 'stalls', 'circle', 'gallery'
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id     SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id  INTEGER REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    placed_at    TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    channel      TEXT NOT NULL,   -- 'web', 'phone', 'counter'
    status       TEXT NOT NULL,   -- 'paid', 'refunded', 'pending'
    total        NUMERIC(8,2)
);

CREATE TABLE tickets (
    ticket_id      SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id       INTEGER REFERENCES orders(order_id),
    performance_id INTEGER REFERENCES performances(performance_id),
    seat_id        INTEGER REFERENCES seats(seat_id),
    price_paid     NUMERIC(8,2) NOT NULL,
    price_band     TEXT,          -- 'full', 'concession', 'under26'
    scanned_at     TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE INDEX idx_tickets_order ON tickets(order_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_customers_name ON customers(lower(full_name));
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders(status);
CREATE INDEX idx_perf_venue ON performances(venue);
CREATE INDEX idx_seats_zone ON seats(zone);
```

Some facts about the data: there are about 140,000 customers, 260,000 orders and 780,000 tickets, growing by roughly 20,000 tickets per month and many more in the first week after a season is announced. The main stage has 640 seats and the studio 90. There are about 150 performances per season. Orders are mostly paid (95%); refunds are 3%. The box office has seen cases of two tickets for the same seat and performance, which should be impossible.

**Query 1: sales per production for the current season**

```sql
SELECT p.title,
       COUNT(t.ticket_id) AS tickets_sold,
       SUM(t.price_paid)  AS revenue
FROM productions p, performances pf, tickets t, orders o
WHERE p.production_id = pf.production_id
  AND pf.performance_id = t.performance_id
  AND t.order_id = o.order_id
  AND o.status <> 'refunded'
  AND p.season = 'Autumn 2026'
GROUP BY p.title
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
```

**Query 2: customers who bought for the autumn season but never for last spring (for a mailing)**

```sql
SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name, c.email
FROM customers c
WHERE c.customer_id IN (
        SELECT o.customer_id FROM orders o, tickets t, performances pf, productions p
        WHERE o.order_id = t.order_id AND t.performance_id = pf.performance_id
          AND pf.production_id = p.production_id AND p.season = 'Autumn 2026')
  AND c.customer_id NOT IN (
        SELECT o.customer_id FROM orders o, tickets t, performances pf, productions p
        WHERE o.order_id = t.order_id AND t.performance_id = pf.performance_id
          AND pf.production_id = p.production_id AND p.season = 'Spring 2026')
  AND c.email LIKE '%@%';
```

**Query 3: occupancy per performance in the last 30 days**

```sql
SELECT pf.performance_id, p.title, pf.starts_at,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tickets t WHERE t.performance_id = pf.performance_id) * 100.0 / pf.capacity AS occupancy_pct
FROM performances pf
JOIN productions p ON p.production_id = pf.production_id
WHERE date(pf.starts_at) >= current_date - 30
  AND date(pf.starts_at) < current_date
ORDER BY occupancy_pct DESC;
```

**Query 4: seats still free for one performance (used by the web booking page on every page load)**

```sql
SELECT s.seat_id, s.row_label, s.seat_no, s.zone
FROM seats s
WHERE s.venue = (SELECT venue FROM performances WHERE performance_id = 4821)
  AND s.seat_id NOT IN (SELECT seat_id FROM tickets WHERE performance_id = 4821)
ORDER BY s.zone, s.row_label, s.seat_no;
```

**Query 5: monthly revenue by channel for the finance report**

```sql
SELECT to_char(o.placed_at, 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
       o.channel,
       SUM(o.total) AS revenue,
       COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders o
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
  AND o.placed_at::date >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY to_char(o.placed_at, 'YYYY-MM'), o.channel
ORDER BY month, o.channel;
```

The finance report is run once a day by the finance manager, and Query 4 runs on every load of the seat map, around 40 times a minute during an on-sale. Query 3 is on the box office dashboard, which refreshes every minute.

Das hier sind die ersten beiden Kapitel meiner Kurzgeschichte. Bitte schreibe sie in demselben ruhigen, leicht ironischen Ton ausführlich weiter, mit mindestens zwei weiteren Kapiteln, und bring die Geschichte zu einem Ende, das zu dem passt, was ich vorbereitet habe.

**Fach 17**

*1*

Die Paketstation am Ende der Kastanienallee hatte siebenundvierzig Fächer, und Ilse Brandtner kannte jedes einzelne davon. Das war nicht übertrieben, es war ihr Beruf. Seit elf Jahren fuhr sie für die Firma Nordkurier Boxen jeden Morgen um sechs Uhr dreißig im weißen Transporter die Runde durch die Stadt, leerte abgelaufene Fächer, füllte Wechselgeld in die Kassenmodule der Rücksendeautomaten nach und putzte die Touchscreens mit einem Tuch, das nach Zitrone roch. Sie hatte dreihundertzwölf Stationen, und sie hätte keine davon freiwillig gegen einen Schreibtisch getauscht.

Es gab Kolleginnen, die den Job als Durchgangsstation betrachteten, bis sich etwas Besseres fand. Ilse fand, dass es nichts Besseres gab. Sie mochte die Stunde vor Sonnenaufgang, wenn die Stadt so tat, als sei sie noch nicht ganz fertig. Sie mochte die Leute, die um diese Zeit an den Stationen standen und mit Rucksack und Kopfhörern auf ein Paket warteten, das sie nicht hatten kommen sehen. Und sie mochte es, dass ein Fach nach dem Zuklappen wieder ein Fach war, mit einer Nummer und einem Zweck, und dass man ihm keine Geschichten zumuten musste. Das war, wie sie später merken sollte, ein Irrtum.

Die Station in der Kastanienallee mochte sie besonders. Sie stand vor einer Bäckerei, die um sieben aufmachte, und wenn Ilse früh genug kam, bekam sie von Herrn Okafor die Brötchen vom Vortag für die Hälfte, was sie nie ablehnte und er nie erwähnte. An diesem Dienstag im Oktober war es kalt, die Kastanien warfen ihre Blätter auf den Gehweg, und sie öffnete das Wartungsfeld mit dem Schlüssel, den sie an einem Band um den Hals trug, so wie man einen Hausschlüssel trägt, wenn man ihn schon einmal verloren hat.

Das System zeigte zwei Fächer als belegt und abgelaufen. Fach 9 enthielt einen Karton mit Gartenschuhen, den ein Kunde seit acht Tagen nicht abgeholt hatte. Fach 17 war leer, aber das Display meldete es als belegt, und das war neu. Ilse drückte auf Prüfen. Das Fach öffnete sich mit dem üblichen Klacken, und darin lag nichts außer einem Zettel, der mit Tesafilm an die Rückwand geklebt war.

Auf dem Zettel stand in sauberer Handschrift: *Bitte nicht öffnen vor dem 31. Oktober. Danke. A.*

Sie las ihn zweimal. Dann tat sie, was sie in elf Jahren noch nie getan hatte: Sie schloss das Fach, setzte sich auf die Kante des Transporters und trank ihren Kaffee, bevor sie jemanden anrief.

*2*

Ihr Vorgesetzter, Dieter Hollenbeck, nahm erst beim dritten Klingeln ab und klang, als habe man ihn aus einer Besprechung gezogen, die er nicht verlassen wollte. „Ein Zettel“, sagte er, nachdem Ilse es erklärt hatte. „Im Fach. Und das Fach ist leer.“

„Es ist leer, und es ist belegt. Beides gleichzeitig.“

„Dann hat sich jemand mit dem Fach verbunden und eine Reservierung gemacht, ohne ein Paket hineinzulegen. Das kann man nicht, aber wenn es geht, dann ist es ein Softwarefehler.“ Er schnaufte. „Mach ein Foto und schick es mir. Und lass den Zettel, wo er ist.“

Ilse machte das Foto. Dann tat sie etwas, das ihr selbst peinlich war: Sie rief im Backoffice an und ließ sich die Reservierung zeigen. Eine Frau namens Svetlana, die Ilse nur von der Stimme kannte, brauchte vier Minuten, um sie zu finden. Das Fach 17 war seit dem 2. September durchgehend reserviert, vom Konto eines Kunden mit der Nummer 40-882-17, und zwar für den Zeitraum bis zum 31. Oktober. Bezahlt war die Reservierung, was es bei Nordkurier gar nicht gab, mit einer Überweisung über 150 Euro an die Firma, mit dem Verwendungszweck „Miete Fach, bitte nicht stören“.

„Das gibt es nicht“, sagte Svetlana. „Wir vermieten keine Fächer. Wir haben keinen Tarif dafür.“

„Offenbar doch.“

„Wer hat das freigeschaltet?“

Eine lange Pause. „Laut Protokoll“, sagte Svetlana langsam, „Herr Hollenbeck. Am 2. September, um 16:40 Uhr. Als Ausnahme.“

Ilse schaute durch die Scheibe der Bäckerei, wo Herr Okafor gerade die Brötchenkörbe ins Regal stellte, und fragte sich, ob sie gerade zur Zeugin einer Dummheit oder eines Plans geworden war. In ihrem Beruf lernte man früh, dass beides oft gleich aussah. Sie bedankte sich, legte auf und rief nicht wieder bei Dieter Hollenbeck an. Herr Okafor winkte durch die Scheibe, und sie ging hinein, weil es einfacher war, als zu erklären, warum nicht. Er legte ihr zwei Brötchen und ein Stück Mohnkuchen in eine Tüte. „Ihr Fach siebzehn“, sagte er beiläufig, „da war neulich ein Mann. Kam abends, kurz vor Ladenschluss, stand lange davor. Hat nichts hineingelegt, nur hineingeschaut. Ein älterer Herr mit einer Aktentasche, die zu groß war für ihn.“ Ilse fragte, ob er ihn kenne. „Nein“, sagte Herr Okafor. „Aber er hat sich bei mir bedankt, als ich ihm die Tür aufgehalten habe, als hätte ich ihm etwas geschenkt. Solche Leute merkt man sich.“

Stattdessen schrieb sie auf ihre Liste für den Tag: *Kastanienallee, 17: nichts tun. Wiederkommen am 31.*

Den Rest der Runde fuhr sie wie immer. Aber in der Frühstückspause, auf dem Parkplatz hinter dem Baumarkt an der Ringstraße, nahm sie den Zettel aus ihrer Jackentasche, dessen Wortlaut sie sich im Transporter noch einmal abgeschrieben hatte, und sah sich die Buchstaben an. Das A. am Schluss. Sie kannte niemanden mit diesem Buchstaben, der sauber schrieb. Fast niemanden. Ihre Mutter hatte Anneliese geheißen, und ihre Mutter war vor sechs Jahren gestorben, und die Handschrift auf dem Zettel hatte, bei aller Vorsicht, mit der Ilse sich solche Gedanken verbot, dieselben Schleifen am großen B.

**Was ich für die Fortsetzung vorbereitet habe:** Ilse findet heraus, dass das Konto 40-882-17 einem Mann gehört, den sie nicht kennt, Matthias Reuter, der eine kleine Uhrmacherwerkstatt am Stadtrand betreibt. Dieter Hollenbeck hat die Ausnahme nicht aus Nachlässigkeit erlaubt, sondern weil Reuter ihm einen Gefallen schuldet. Am 31. Oktober, an Ilses Geburtstag, soll sich zeigen, wer das Fach tatsächlich braucht und warum. Der Ton soll weiter freundlich und trocken bleiben, ohne Krimi-Effekte. Es darf am Ende ein wenig rührend sein, aber nicht kitschig.

I need a review of this database design, including whether the indexes make sense, and I would like the slow queries rewritten with an explanation of why each rewrite is better. This is the schema for our haulage and blasting records at Greywacke Ridge quarry, running on PostgreSQL. The weighbridge report takes almost a minute now and the planners keep complaining about the monthly tonnage query.

```sql
CREATE TABLE sites (
    site_id      serial PRIMARY KEY,
    name         text NOT NULL,
    permit_no    text NOT NULL,
    max_daily_t  integer NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE products (
    product_id   serial PRIMARY KEY,
    code         text NOT NULL,
    description  text,
    price_per_t  numeric(8,2) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id  serial PRIMARY KEY,
    name         text NOT NULL,
    account_ref  text,
    credit_limit numeric(10,2) DEFAULT 0
);

CREATE TABLE trucks (
    truck_id     serial PRIMARY KEY,
    plate        text NOT NULL,
    haulier      text,
    tare_kg      integer NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE loads (
    load_id      bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    site_id      integer REFERENCES sites(site_id),
    product_id   integer REFERENCES products(product_id),
    customer_id  integer REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    truck_id     integer REFERENCES trucks(truck_id),
    gross_kg     integer NOT NULL,
    weighed_at   timestamp NOT NULL,
    ticket_no    text,
    status       text DEFAULT 'open'
);

CREATE TABLE blasts (
    blast_id     serial PRIMARY KEY,
    site_id      integer REFERENCES sites(site_id),
    fired_at     timestamp NOT NULL,
    holes        integer,
    explosive_kg numeric(8,1),
    fired_by     text,
    notes        text
);

CREATE TABLE complaints (
    complaint_id serial PRIMARY KEY,
    blast_id     integer REFERENCES blasts(blast_id),
    received_at  timestamp NOT NULL,
    postcode     text,
    description  text,
    resolved     boolean DEFAULT false
);

CREATE INDEX idx_loads_weighed ON loads (weighed_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_loads_status ON loads (status);
CREATE INDEX idx_blasts_fired ON blasts (fired_at);
```

Here are the queries that hurt.

```sql
-- 1. Monthly tonnage by product for the permit return
SELECT p.code,
       to_char(l.weighed_at, 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
       sum(l.gross_kg - t.tare_kg) / 1000.0 AS net_tonnes
FROM loads l
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = l.product_id
JOIN trucks t ON t.truck_id = l.truck_id
WHERE to_char(l.weighed_at, 'YYYY') = '2026'
GROUP BY p.code, to_char(l.weighed_at, 'YYYY-MM')
ORDER BY month, p.code;

-- 2. Customers over their credit limit this month
SELECT c.name,
       (SELECT sum((l.gross_kg - t.tare_kg) / 1000.0 * p.price_per_t)
          FROM loads l
          JOIN trucks t ON t.truck_id = l.truck_id
          JOIN products p ON p.product_id = l.product_id
         WHERE l.customer_id = c.customer_id
           AND l.weighed_at >= date_trunc('month', now())) AS owed
FROM customers c
WHERE (SELECT sum((l.gross_kg - t.tare_kg) / 1000.0 * p.price_per_t)
         FROM loads l
         JOIN trucks t ON t.truck_id = l.truck_id
         JOIN products p ON p.product_id = l.product_id
        WHERE l.customer_id = c.customer_id
          AND l.weighed_at >= date_trunc('month', now())) > c.credit_limit;

-- 3. Days we went over the permit's daily limit
SELECT s.name, l.weighed_at::date AS day, sum(l.gross_kg - t.tare_kg) / 1000 AS tonnes
FROM loads l, sites s, trucks t
WHERE l.site_id = s.site_id AND l.truck_id = t.truck_id
GROUP BY s.name, s.max_daily_t, l.weighed_at::date
HAVING sum(l.gross_kg - t.tare_kg) / 1000 > s.max_daily_t;

-- 4. Blasts with unresolved complaints in the last 90 days
SELECT b.blast_id, b.fired_at, count(*)
FROM blasts b
LEFT JOIN complaints c ON c.blast_id = b.blast_id
WHERE c.resolved = false
  AND b.fired_at > now() - interval '90 days'
GROUP BY b.blast_id, b.fired_at;

-- 5. Open tickets older than a week
SELECT * FROM loads WHERE status = 'open' AND ticket_no LIKE '%GR%'
  AND weighed_at < now() - interval '7 days';

-- 6. Busiest haulier per product over the last quarter
SELECT p.code, t.haulier, count(*) AS trips
FROM loads l
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = l.product_id
JOIN trucks t ON t.truck_id = l.truck_id
WHERE l.weighed_at >= now() - interval '3 months'
GROUP BY p.code, t.haulier
HAVING count(*) = (
    SELECT max(c) FROM (
        SELECT count(*) AS c
        FROM loads l2
        JOIN trucks t2 ON t2.truck_id = l2.truck_id
        WHERE l2.product_id = l.product_id
          AND l2.weighed_at >= now() - interval '3 months'
        GROUP BY t2.haulier
    ) x
);

-- 7. Explosive used per tonne shipped, by site and month
SELECT s.name,
       to_char(b.fired_at, 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
       sum(b.explosive_kg) AS explosive,
       (SELECT sum(l.gross_kg) / 1000.0 FROM loads l
         WHERE l.site_id = b.site_id
           AND to_char(l.weighed_at, 'YYYY-MM') = to_char(b.fired_at, 'YYYY-MM')) AS shipped_t
FROM blasts b
JOIN sites s ON s.site_id = b.site_id
GROUP BY s.name, b.site_id, to_char(b.fired_at, 'YYYY-MM');
```

For scale, the loads table has about 4.1 million rows and grows by roughly 1,800 a day across three sites. Blasts number a few thousand and complaints a few hundred. Almost every load is eventually marked closed, so the open status is rare. The permit return is filed once a month, but the credit check runs every time a driver reaches the weighbridge.

Here is a design document our furnace team wrote for a new kiln monitoring system at Tarnside Glassworks. Can you critique it honestly, suggest at least two alternative approaches we should have considered, and then give me an implementation plan I can take to the next planning meeting? I am the plant engineer and I have to sign it off, but I am not a software person, so explain the risks in terms I can act on.

# Design: Kiln Watch, continuous temperature and energy monitoring

Author: Imogen Pryce (furnace systems). Reviewers: Dalton Reeve (plant engineer), Sunita Marsh (production manager). Status: draft 3.

## 1. Background

Tarnside runs one regenerative melting furnace (Furnace 1, container glass, 140 tonnes per day) and four annealing lehrs. Today an operator walks the line every two hours and writes thermocouple readings from the local displays on a clipboard. The numbers are typed into a spreadsheet at the end of the shift. This has three problems. First, a lehr that drifts out of its annealing curve between walks produces stressed bottles that are only found at the cold-end inspection, hours later. Second, we cannot show the gas supplier or the auditor any trend finer than two hours. Third, the furnace crown temperature is the number that most affects refractory life, and nobody sees it for long stretches of the night shift.

In the last twelve months we scrapped roughly 3.1 percent of output for annealing defects, of which we estimate about a third could have been caught by earlier warning. Gas consumption was 8 percent above the contract baseline in February, and we could not explain it.

## 2. Goals

- Record temperature at every existing thermocouple at least once every 10 seconds.
- Record gas flow and electric boost power every 10 seconds.
- Alert the shift supervisor within 60 seconds when a lehr zone leaves its tolerance band for more than 90 seconds.
- Keep one year of full-resolution history and five years of one-minute averages.
- Show the supervisor a single screen with the state of the furnace and all four lehrs.

## 3. Non-goals

- Closed-loop control. Kiln Watch only observes. The existing control cabinets stay in charge of heating.
- Replacing the existing local displays.
- Predicting defects with machine learning. This may be a later phase.

## 4. Proposed architecture

Each of the five areas gets a small edge box (a fanless industrial computer) mounted in the control cabinet. The box reads the thermocouples through an analog input module over Modbus, polls the gas flow meter and the boost transformer over Modbus TCP, and buffers readings in a local queue on disk. Every 10 seconds the box sends a batch to a central server in the office server room over the plant network. The central server runs a time series database, an alert service and a web dashboard. Alerts go by SMS and by email to the supervisor on duty, who is looked up in a rota table.

Edge boxes keep up to 72 hours of readings if the network is down and forward them in order when it returns. Timestamps are taken at the edge box, which is synchronised to the central server by NTP.

### 4.1 Data model

One measurement record is: area, sensor id, timestamp, value, unit and quality flag. Tolerance bands are stored per sensor with a lower and upper limit and a hold time. Bands for the lehrs follow the annealing schedule for the product currently running, so a band changes when the product changes. The product schedule is entered by the supervisor on the dashboard at each job change.

### 4.2 Alerting

The alert service evaluates each sensor every 10 seconds against the band for the active product. A breach starts a timer. If the value stays outside the band for the hold time, an alert is raised. Alerts are acknowledged on the dashboard; an unacknowledged alert repeats every 5 minutes and, after 15 minutes, goes to the plant engineer as well. When a value returns inside the band for 60 seconds the alert clears.

### 4.3 Dashboard

The dashboard is a web page served from the central server and shown on a wall display in the control room and on supervisors' tablets. It shows a plan view of the furnace and lehrs with colour-coded zones, a 12-hour trend per zone, current gas use against the daily target, and the list of open alerts.

## 5. Hardware and cost

| Item | Quantity | Unit cost | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Edge box with Modbus interfaces | 5 | 1,150 | 5,750 |
| Analog input modules (8 channel thermocouple) | 12 | 420 | 5,040 |
| Central server with mirrored disks | 1 | 3,900 | 3,900 |
| Wall display and two tablets | 1 set | 1,800 | 1,800 |
| Cabling and cabinet work | 1 lot | 4,500 | 4,500 |
| Installation labour (contractor) | 1 lot | 6,000 | 6,000 |
| Total | | | 27,000 |

Software is written in house by Imogen with about 60 days of effort, using open source components. There is no budget line for support after go-live.

## 6. Rollout

Phase 1 (weeks 1 to 4): install on Lehr 3 only, run in parallel with the clipboard. Phase 2 (weeks 5 to 8): extend to the remaining lehrs. Phase 3 (weeks 9 to 12): furnace crown, regenerators and gas. The clipboard round stops only after four weeks of clean parallel running on all areas.

## 7. Security and safety

The edge boxes sit on the plant network, which shares a switch with the office network. Access to the dashboard is by a shared supervisor login. The system has no write path to the control cabinets. Modbus polling is read-only, and the polling accounts are configured with read function codes only.

## 8. Risks identified so far

1. Thermocouple cold-junction drift may make logged values differ from the local displays. Mitigation: calibrate at install against a reference.
2. Operators may forget to enter the product schedule, leaving the wrong band active. Mitigation: a reminder at job change.
3. SMS gateway outage. Mitigation: email fallback.
4. A single central server is a single point of failure for alerting. Mitigation: nightly backups.

## 9. Open questions

- Who owns the system after go-live, and who is on call when an alert fires at 3 a.m.?
- Should one year of full-resolution history be kept on the server disks or archived?
- Do we need the auditor to approve the data before it is used as evidence of gas consumption?

## 10. Success measure

After six months, scrap for annealing defects falls below 2.3 percent and the gas overrun against baseline is explained within a day of occurring.

This agreement is made on 2 October 2026 between Wenslow Fold Dairy Ltd, whose registered office is at Fold Farm, Wenslow Bank, Eastmere (the "Supplier"), and Candlewick Provisions Ltd, whose registered office is at Unit 9, Harbour Yard, Northquay (the "Buyer").

I would like a detailed peer review of the methods and results section below, written as if you were a referee for a journal on heritage management. Please comment on the design, the statistics, whether the conclusions follow from the evidence, and what the authors should add or change. Be specific, point to numbers, and end with a recommendation and a ranked list of required revisions.

**Does repainting on a fixed cycle protect coastal lighthouse towers? A comparison of maintenance regimes across 14 sites**

*Methods and Results (draft 2, for the Skerrow Lighthouse Trust)*

**2. Methods**

2.1 Sites. The Skerrow Lighthouse Trust cares for 14 decommissioned light towers on the north and east coasts. All are masonry towers between 11 and 31 m tall, built between 1847 and 1912. Exposure was rated from 1 (sheltered estuary) to 5 (open sea) by the Trust's surveyor using fetch distance and recorded storm days. Eight towers have exposure 4 or 5.

2.2 Maintenance regimes. Between 2014 and 2019 the Trust followed one of two regimes. Seven towers (Group A) were repainted with a lime-based breathable coating every four years. The other seven (Group B) were repainted every eight years with an acrylic masonry paint, after the Trust's former contractor argued that the acrylic would last twice as long. Allocation was not random: the Trust gave Group A to the towers that its volunteers could reach most easily, because the lime coating needs more frequent work.

2.3 Outcome measures. In June 2024 a single surveyor inspected each tower and recorded three outcomes. (i) Moisture: the mean of 12 readings with a resistance moisture meter at 1.5 m on the leeward face, expressed as percent by weight. (ii) Salt: the surface chloride content from three scrapings per tower, measured in the laboratory in mg per kg. (iii) Defect count: the number of cracks wider than 0.3 mm, spalled areas larger than 100 cm2 and loose joints counted over the whole tower, divided by the wall area in square metres.

2.4 Analysis. Group means were compared with Welch's t test. We also fitted a linear regression of the defect rate on group, exposure and tower age. Because of the small sample, the significance level was set at 0.10. Missing data were handled by dropping the tower from that analysis. All analysis was done in a spreadsheet.

2.5 Measurement quality. The moisture meter was calibrated against an oven-dried core from one tower before the survey, and the readings were converted using the manufacturer's curve for sandstone. Eleven of the towers are sandstone and three (Brae Head, Cullen Point and Inner Skerry) are brick. The brick towers were measured with the same curve. Defects were counted in a single pass from ground level and from the gallery, and no ladders or drones were used above the lantern room.

**3. Results**

3.1 Sample. All 14 towers were surveyed. For one tower (Hallen Ness, Group B) the laboratory lost the salt samples, leaving 13 towers for the chloride analysis. Mean age was 128 years in Group A and 109 years in Group B. Mean exposure was 3.0 in Group A and 4.1 in Group B.

3.2 Moisture. Mean moisture was 14.2 percent (standard deviation 3.1) in Group A and 17.9 percent (standard deviation 4.0) in Group B. The difference of 3.7 percentage points was significant (t = 1.95, p = 0.08). Moisture rose with exposure in both groups.

3.3 Salt. Mean surface chloride was 410 mg per kg in Group A (n = 7) and 655 mg per kg in Group B (n = 6). The difference was not significant (p = 0.21), although the direction agrees with the moisture result. The two highest values, 1,240 and 1,090 mg per kg, were both from Group B towers on exposed headlands.

3.4 Defects. The mean defect rate was 0.42 per square metre in Group A and 0.81 per square metre in Group B. In the regression model the coefficient for Group B was 0.31 (95 percent confidence interval 0.02 to 0.60). The coefficient for exposure was 0.18 per unit (p = 0.03) and tower age was not significant. The model explained 61 percent of the variance (adjusted R2 = 0.49).

3.5 Costs. Over the 2014 to 2024 period, the lime regime cost an average of 19,400 per tower in materials and contractor time and the acrylic regime cost an average of 14,900 per tower. The Trust's volunteers contributed an estimated 310 hours per tower to Group A and 120 hours per tower to Group B, which are not included in the figures above.

3.6 Results by exposure. To check whether the group difference was an artefact of exposure, towers were divided into sheltered (exposure 1 to 3) and exposed (exposure 4 to 5) sets. Mean defect rates per square metre are shown below.

| Exposure set | Group A (lime, 4 years) | Group B (acrylic, 8 years) |
|---|---|---|
| Sheltered | 0.35 (n = 5) | 0.38 (n = 1) |
| Exposed | 0.60 (n = 2) | 0.88 (n = 6) |

Among exposed towers Group B had the higher defect rate, by 0.28 per square metre. Among sheltered towers there was only one Group B tower, so no comparison was attempted.

3.7 Summary of findings. Towers repainted every four years with lime had less moisture, lower chloride and fewer defects than towers repainted every eight years with acrylic paint, although only the moisture and defect differences reached the 0.10 level. The acrylic regime was cheaper in cash terms but, after adjustment for exposure, was associated with about 0.3 additional defects per square metre. We therefore conclude that breathable lime coatings on a four-year cycle protect coastal masonry better than acrylic coatings on an eight-year cycle, and that the Trust should move all towers to the lime regime. Because the defect rate rose with exposure, towers rated 4 or 5 should be repainted first.

3.8 Limitations. The towers were not randomly allocated, and the surveyor was aware of each tower's regime. The study has a single inspection time point, so we cannot say how fast defects accumulated. Hallen Ness, the tower with missing salt data, is also the most exposed in Group B.

Here are the first two chapters of a short story I am writing. Please continue it at length in the same voice, with at least two more chapters, and bring it to a proper ending. Keep the quiet, slightly dry tone, keep the details consistent with what is already there, and let the factory itself matter to how things turn out.

THE LAST WOODEN HORSE

1.

On the morning the order came, Odile Fennimore was sanding the left hind leg of a rocking horse and thinking about nothing at all, which was how she liked to begin the day.

The Pettibone Toy Works stood at the bottom of Cutler's Hill, where the road gave up and became a footpath to the canal. It had been a brewery once, and the smell had never quite left; on damp days the paint shop still gave off a note of old hops, and the older workers claimed that the glue held better because of it. There were forty-one people on the payroll in the spring, which was down from a hundred and ten when Odile started as a girl of sixteen, and in the long upstairs room where the horses were made there were now only three benches in use out of twelve. The other nine were covered with dust sheets, like furniture in a house that is being sold.

She heard Mr. Garrow's footsteps before she saw him. He walked with the heavy care of a man carrying something that might spill, and he was carrying nothing but a single sheet of paper.

"Odile," he said. "A moment."

She put down the sanding block and blew the dust off her wrists. At the next bench Tobias, who was nineteen and had been sent to them by the council's training scheme, stopped pretending to look at a joint.

"It's Harcourt and Vane," Mr. Garrow said. "They want six hundred."

"Six hundred what?"

"Horses. The big pattern, the dapple grey, with the real horsehair tail. For the autumn catalogue. They want them in the warehouse by the second of October."

Odile did the sum without meaning to, as she did all sums, with her lips slightly pressed. The shop could make eleven horses a week when nothing went wrong and the glue was kind. It was the ninth of August.

"That's seven weeks," she said. "Seventy-seven horses, if we are lucky."

"Yes."

"They know that."

"They do not know that," said Mr. Garrow. "They know that they ordered forty last year and we delivered forty. They have looked at a spreadsheet and seen that the number can be made bigger." He laid the paper on her bench, carefully, as though it too might spill. "They are offering a price that would pay for the roof."

Both of them looked up. There was a place above the paint shop where a bucket sat all winter on a plank, and neither of them mentioned it.

"And if we say no?"

"They go to the factory in the east. The one with the machines. And we do not get asked again."

Odile picked up the paper and read it twice, once for the numbers and once for the tone, which was friendly in the way of someone who has already decided. At the bottom was a name, Ms. Imre Calloway, Head of Seasonal Buying, and a line of small print saying that horses must be, quote, of consistent finish and delivered in carton packs of six.

"Consistent finish," she said.

"I know."

"Every horse I've made has a different face. That is the whole reason people want them."

"I know, Odile," said Mr. Garrow, and he looked, for a moment, very tired. "I'm only the man who brought it up the stairs."

2.

By lunchtime the whole building knew. News in the Pettibone Toy Works did not travel by gossip so much as by vibration; you could feel it pass through the floor, from the stairs to the packing room to the yard, where the delivery lorry driver put out his cigarette and asked what had happened.

They held the meeting in the canteen because it was the only room with enough chairs. Mr. Garrow stood by the tea urn. Beside him was his daughter Priya, who kept the books and who had come home from a job in the city three years ago with a quiet expression and a laptop that she guarded like a pet.

"I have done the figures," Priya said. "I will say them once, and then you can argue with them. If we take the order and we hit it, we are secure for two years. If we take it and we miss, Harcourt and Vane do not pay for anything late and the penalty clause is eight percent of the whole order. That is about the cost of two of the three benches that are still running."

"So we do not miss," said Bernard from the paint shop, who was sixty-seven and had a voice like gravel in a tin.

"We cannot make six hundred horses by hand in seven weeks, Bernard. We could not do it with twelve benches."

"Then we need machines," said Tobias, and everyone looked at him.

He went red but did not stop. "There's a router at the college. A numerical one. It cuts the body from a block in twenty minutes. I did a unit on it. The council course has a loan scheme for small firms and the college would lend us the machine for evenings."

There was a silence in which the urn ticked.

"A router does not make a horse," said Odile.

"No. But it makes the parts, and you could put them together. And paint them. And you do the faces."

"Consistent finish," said Bernard, and spat the words like a seed.

Odile did not answer at once. She was looking at the long windows along the canteen wall, where the light came in grey from the canal, and thinking about her father, who had carved the first of the dapple greys in 1961 from the trunk of a pear tree that had fallen in the vicarage garden. He had said that a horse was finished when it looked as though it was about to be let go. She had never been able to explain that to anyone who asked how long a horse took.

"Tell me what the college has," she said at last.

Tobias told her. It was a machine the size of a small car, and it had been used for chair legs and for the school's rocket club. It could not do the head, which had too many curves, but it could do the barrel and the four legs and the rocker, and it could cut them so that each fitted with a tongue and a groove without a drop of glue. Priya was writing as he spoke. Mr. Garrow had sat down.

"Two hundred and fifty horses from the machine, perhaps," Priya said when he had finished. "Plus our seventy-seven by hand. That is not six hundred."

"No," said Odile. "But it is more than I thought a minute ago."

She got up. Her knees ached from the stairs, as they always did in August, when the damp came off the canal.

"Mr. Garrow," she said. "Ring Ms. Calloway. Ask her what 'consistent' means to her. Ask her if she has ever held one."

MODULE 3: SIZING AND STRINGING A DOMESTIC ROOF SYSTEM
Lecturer: Ines Valdarno. Two main sessions, Tuesday and Thursday, plus an optional evening class.

SESSION 1 - HOW MUCH SYSTEM DOES THE HOUSE NEED?

1. Start with the customer, not the roof
- First question is always annual electricity use in kWh, from twelve months of bills. Do not use one bill. A house that is empty in August looks very different from one with a teenager at home.
- Typical home in our area: 3,800 kWh per year. A house with an electric car: add 2,000 to 3,000 kWh.
- Ines says the roof sets the limit, but the bills set the target. If the target is bigger than the roof can carry, say so honestly and do not oversell.

2. Rule of thumb for yield
- In our region one kilowatt peak (kWp) of panels facing south at 35 degrees makes about 950 kWh per year.
- Other directions lose some of that. Table she gave us (percent of the best case):
  - South, 35 degrees: 100
  - South-east or south-west, 35 degrees: 95
  - East or west, 35 degrees: 85
  - South, flat roof (10 degrees): 91
  - North, 35 degrees: 60 (we do not usually fit this)
- Shading takes more off. Light shading from a chimney in the morning: knock off 5. A tree that shades the array through the middle of the day: 15 to 25, and we should think about optimisers.

3. Worked example 1 (done in class)
- Customer: Mr Adeyemi-Roche. Uses 4,200 kWh a year. Roof faces south-west at 35 degrees, no shading.
- Yield per kWp = 950 x 0.95 = 902.5 kWh per year.
- To cover 100 percent of use: 4,200 / 902.5 = 4.65 kWp.
- We do not size to 100 percent, because the house does not use power when the sun shines. Ines suggests aiming for 80 to 90 percent of annual use for a normal family out at work. At 85 percent: 4,200 x 0.85 = 3,570 kWh, which needs 3,570 / 902.5 = 3.96 kWp, so we round to 4.0 kWp.
- Panel choice: 400 W panels. 4,000 / 400 = 10 panels.
- Estimated output: 4.0 x 902.5 = 3,610 kWh per year.

4. Self-consumption and export
- Self-consumption means the share of solar output used in the house at the time it is made. Without a battery a typical family uses about 35 percent. With a 5 kWh battery about 60 percent. With a 10 kWh battery about 75 percent.
- Example 1 again, no battery: 3,610 x 0.35 = 1,264 kWh used in the house and 3,610 - 1,264 = 2,346 kWh exported.
- Money: the customer pays 28 pence for each unit bought and is paid 12 pence for each unit exported. Saving = 1,264 x 0.28 = 353.92 pounds. Export income = 2,346 x 0.12 = 281.52 pounds. Total benefit = 635.44 pounds per year.
- Installed cost quoted for 4.0 kWp with no battery: 6,400 pounds. Simple payback = 6,400 / 635.44 = 10.07 years. Ines said we should say "about ten years" and not "10.07 years", because bills and tariffs change.

5. Roof checks before we promise anything
- Structure: rafter size and spacing, condition of the tiles and battens, and weight. A panel and rail weigh about 12 to 15 kg per square metre. NOTE for myself: I wrote 15 kg per panel in class, but the slides say 18 kg per panel and about 11 kg per square metre once the load is spread out. The slides are right.
- Space: each 400 W panel is 1.76 m by 1.13 m. Keep 0.4 m clear from the ridge and 0.3 m from the edges for access and wind.
- Wind and snow loads come from the site survey. Ask for the structural engineer if the roof is old or the rafters are under 100 mm deep.

SESSION 2 - STRINGS, INVERTERS AND SAFETY

6. Electrical basics we need
- Voltage (V), current (A), power (W) = V x A.
- Panels in series add voltage and keep the same current. Panels in parallel add current and keep the same voltage.
- A group of panels in series is called a string.
- Panel data for the 400 W panels we use (at standard conditions): Voc (open circuit voltage) 41.2 V, Vmp (voltage at max power) 34.5 V, Isc (short circuit current) 12.3 A, Imp 11.6 A.
- Check: 34.5 x 11.6 = 400.2 W. Good.

7. Why temperature matters
- Cold makes voltage go UP. On a frosty bright morning the string voltage is higher than the label says. The panel loses 0.27 percent of voltage per degree Celsius above 25, and gains the same below 25.
- Coldest design temperature for our region: minus 10 degrees. That is 35 degrees below 25.
- Voc at minus 10 = 41.2 x (1 + 0.0027 x 35) = 41.2 x 1.0945 = 45.09 V.
- Hot roofs make voltage go DOWN. Hottest design cell temperature: 70 degrees, that is 45 above 25. Vmp at 70 = 34.5 x (1 - 0.0027 x 45) = 34.5 x 0.8785 = 30.31 V.

8. Matching the string to the inverter
- Inverter in the worked example: 4.0 kW single phase string inverter. Max input voltage 600 V. MPPT range 120 V to 550 V. Start voltage 150 V. Max input current 16 A per input.
- Rule A: the cold Voc of the whole string must stay below the max input voltage. 600 / 45.09 = 13.3 so at most 13 panels per string.
- Rule B: the hot Vmp of the string must stay above the bottom of the MPPT range. 120 / 30.31 = 3.96 so at least 4 panels. In practice we want a safety margin and the start voltage matters too: 150 / 30.31 = 4.9, so at least 5.
- Rule C: the current must stay below the max input current. Isc 12.3 A is below 16 A. Fine.
- Our 10 panels in one string: cold Voc = 450.9 V (under 600), hot Vmp = 303.1 V (well inside 120 to 550). One string works.
- Ines asked us what happens if the roof is split in two faces. Answer: use two strings on two separate inputs (two MPPT trackers), because panels facing different ways peak at different times and one tracker cannot serve both. For example 6 panels on the south-west face and 4 on the north-west face would be two strings.

9. Cables and protection
- DC cable: 4 mm squared, double insulated, solar-rated. Keep the voltage drop on the DC side below 1 percent and on the AC side below 1 percent.
- Voltage drop (rough) = 2 x length x current x resistance per metre. 4 mm squared copper is 0.0046 ohm per metre. Example: 20 m run, 11.6 A. Drop = 2 x 20 x 11.6 x 0.0046 = 2.13 V. Compared with a string at about 345 V (10 x 34.5) that is 2.13 / 345 = 0.62 percent, which passes.
- A DC isolator next to the inverter, and one at the array if the cable run is longer than 30 m.
- AC side: a 20 A breaker on a dedicated circuit for a 4 kW inverter, 4 mm squared cable if the run is under 20 m. 4,000 W / 230 V = 17.4 A so a 20 A breaker is fine.
- Earth: all metal frames bonded with 6 mm squared green and yellow cable. The earth bond is checked on the final test sheet.

10. Safety on the roof
- Work at height rules: scaffold for any roof edge over 2 m from the ground, and we never work alone on a roof.
- DC cannot be switched off while the sun shines. Cover the panels with the black cloth bags if you must work on live connections, but treat every connector as live anyway.
- Never unplug a connector under load. Turn off the AC and DC isolators first, wait five minutes for the inverter to discharge, then check with the meter.
- Fire services need to see a label at the meter, one at the consumer unit and one at the inverter saying "solar PV installed".

11. Testing before handover
- Open circuit voltage of each string: should be within 5 percent of the calculated value for the day's temperature.
- Insulation resistance test at 1,000 V DC: must be over 1 megohm.
- Earth continuity: under 0.5 ohm between any frame and the main earth.
- Then switch on, watch the inverter start, and record power after ten minutes. Compare with expected output from irradiance. If you get less than 85 percent of expected, look for shading, a loose connector, or a wrongly set country code on the inverter.

SESSION 3 (OPTIONAL EVENING CLASS) - BATTERIES AND PAPERWORK

12. Does a battery pay?
- Same house as example 1 (Mr Adeyemi-Roche, 4.0 kWp, 3,610 kWh per year). Add a 5 kWh battery, which lifts self-consumption from 35 to 60 percent.
- Used in the house: 3,610 x 0.60 = 2,166 kWh. Exported: 3,610 - 2,166 = 1,444 kWh.
- Saving = 2,166 x 0.28 = 606.48 pounds. Export income = 1,444 x 0.12 = 173.28 pounds. Total = 779.76 pounds per year.
- Extra benefit from the battery = 779.76 - 635.44 = 144.32 pounds per year.
- The battery costs 2,900 pounds fitted, so on savings alone it pays back in 2,900 / 144.32 = 20.1 years. Ines said most batteries are guaranteed for ten years, so on these numbers it does not pay for itself unless the customer has a time-of-use tariff, expects prices to rise a lot, or values having power in a cut.
- Her advice: never promise the customer that a battery will "pay for itself". Say what it does (shifts use to the evening and gives some backup) and show the numbers.

13. Choosing a battery size
- Look at evening use. A family that uses 8 kWh between 5pm and midnight does not need a 15 kWh battery. A 5 to 7 kWh battery will be full most days in summer and half full in winter.
- Check that the battery inverter can deliver enough power. A 3 kW output will run lights, fridge and TV but not an electric shower at the same time.
- Backup mode needs a separate small consumer unit for the circuits that must stay on. That is extra cost and extra labour, and many customers do not know about it until after the quote.

14. Paperwork and the grid
- Systems up to 3.68 kW per phase can be connected on a "notify after" basis: we tell the network operator within 28 days of commissioning. Bigger systems, like our 4.0 kW example, need permission BEFORE we connect, which takes up to 45 days. This is the most common cause of delay in our jobs.
- The customer receives: an electrical installation certificate, the commissioning sheet with the string test results, the inverter and panel warranty papers, the roof penetration warranty, and a one-page "how to read your inverter" guide.
- We keep our own copy of all of it for seven years.
- Registration for the export payment is done by the customer, but we help them with the form and the meter reading on the day.

Things Ines said would definitely be in the assessment: the yield table, the string voltage maths with temperature, the rule A/B/C check, and the three tests before handover.

HARROWGATE COUNTY RECORDS ARCHIVE
STEERING GROUP - MINUTES
Date: Wednesday 14 October 2026, 10:00 to 12:20, Reading Room Annexe
Present: Philippa Dunmore (County Archivist, chair), Tomasz Reyes (Head of Conservation), Aisha Venkataraman (Digital Programme Manager), Colm Ferreira (Facilities), Yvette Strand (Finance Business Partner), Godfrey Alabi (Public Services Lead), Rhiannon Oakes (volunteer coordinator), Bram Kessel (IT, joined at item 3)
Apologies: Dr Sunniva Hale (Friends of the Archive)
Minutes: Rhiannon Oakes

1. Minutes of the last meeting and matters arising

1.1 Minutes of 9 September agreed as a true record.
1.2 Matters arising: the fire survey of the old boiler room has been done. Colm reported that the room can hold the 220 metres of shelving the group wants, but the sprinkler pipework must be moved first. Quote received for 11,400 pounds. Action on Colm to confirm the quote is firm (see item 5).
1.3 The grant letter from the Heritage Trust arrived on 28 September. The Trust will pay 186,000 pounds in total, in three instalments: 40 percent on signing, 40 percent at the half way report, 20 percent on the final report. Yvette said the final report must be in by 30 June 2027 or the last instalment is lost.

2. The project in outline

2.1 Philippa reminded the group of the scope agreed in the grant bid: (a) digitise the parish registers 1538 to 1900 (about 412 volumes, estimated 61,800 images) and the quarter sessions rolls 1620 to 1830 (about 96 boxes, estimated 38,500 images); (b) put the images online with a searchable index; (c) move the public reading room from the damp east wing into the old boiler room area and open it in the new space.
2.2 The group agreed the project start date is Monday 2 November 2026 and the end date is 30 June 2027, set by the grant.
2.3 Tomasz asked whether the 1538 registers are fit to be scanned. Condition survey so far covers only 140 of 412 volumes. Tomasz expects that between 10 and 15 percent will need repair before scanning. He said a volume needing repair takes about 6 hours of conservator time.

3. Digitisation

3.1 Aisha presented the scanning plan. Two overhead book scanners will be hired from a supplier for six months, at 1,650 pounds per month each. A third scanner is in the budget as a spare but Aisha is not sure it is needed. Agreed to decide at the half way point.
3.2 Throughput: Aisha's pilot last month showed that one trained operator on one scanner makes about 480 images in a seven hour day for registers and about 360 for the rolls, because the rolls need to be unrolled and flattened. Working days available between 4 January and 28 May: 100 (excluding bank holidays and the Easter closure).
3.3 Aisha's calculation: registers 61,800 / 480 = 128.75 operator days; rolls 38,500 / 360 = 106.9 operator days. Total about 236 operator days. With two scanners running on 100 days that is 200 operator days, so the group is about 36 days short. Options discussed: (a) a third scanner for the last 60 days; (b) Saturday working by volunteers; (c) drop the lowest priority 18th century rolls. No decision. Philippa asked Aisha to bring costed options to the next meeting.
3.4 Bram joined. He confirmed the storage server can take 100 TB, which is enough for the master images (about 55 TB at the chosen format) with room for copies. A second copy will go to the offsite store in the neighbouring county. He needs the file naming rules from Aisha by 20 November to set up the folders.
3.5 The online index: Godfrey said that the public wants a name search above all. The supplier of the catalogue software has quoted 22,500 pounds for a transcription module. Rhiannon said volunteers could do transcription of the 1813 to 1837 registers, which are the best loved by family historians, but nobody has agreed how many volunteers can be found. She estimates 25 in the first year based on the current list of 41 people who have asked to help.
3.6 Bram raised a concern about the supplier's hosting terms, which require the Trust grant to pay three years in advance (31,800 pounds). Yvette said the Trust may not allow that because costs after 30 June 2027 are not eligible. To be checked with the Trust officer.

4. Conservation

4.1 Tomasz said that repair of the 1538 to 1640 registers will be done by himself and one part time conservator, Lucia Ferreira-Nwosu, who is available three days a week from 1 December. At 412 volumes with 12.5 percent needing repair (say 52 volumes) at 6 hours each, the repair time is 312 hours, or about 45 working days of one person at seven hours a day. At three days a week Lucia alone would take 15 weeks, so Tomasz will do part of it himself.
4.2 The conservator's time is already in the budget at 31,200 pounds for the project. Tomasz thinks this is enough only if the percentage needing repair is 15 or below.
4.3 Rolls: 12 of the 96 boxes are known to be mouldy. Tomasz said that they must be dry cleaned off site by a specialist before anyone handles them. A specialist visit costs 2,100 pounds per day and he expects two days. The mouldy boxes cannot be scanned until this is done. He suggested to do this in November so that the rolls can be scanned from February.
4.4 The group noted that the new shelving room must be climate controlled before any records move. Colm said the climate control unit has a lead time of 10 weeks.

5. Reading room move

5.1 Colm presented the facilities plan. Work order: (1) move the sprinkler pipework (11,400 pounds, 3 weeks); (2) install the climate control unit (48,000 pounds, 10 week lead time and 1 week fitting); (3) install the 220 metres of shelving (36,500 pounds, 2 weeks); (4) paint and floor (9,200 pounds, 2 weeks); (5) move the records in a controlled way over 2 weeks; (6) install reading room furniture and the new public access computers (14,000 pounds, 1 week).
5.2 Colm said that if he places the climate unit order on 20 October, delivery would be by 29 December and the full facilities work could be done by 26 February 2027 if the sprinkler job starts on 9 November and nothing slips. The records could move from 1 March for two weeks. The reading room could open on Monday 22 March 2027, and the damp east wing could close after that.
5.3 Godfrey said that readers use the room most in March and April (Easter and school holidays) and does not want a closure at that time. He wants a plan for a two week closure in January or in May instead. Philippa pointed out that the sprinkler work and records move cannot be shifted without moving the whole date. No decision. Philippa will talk to the Friends before the next meeting.
5.4 Yvette asked about contingency. Philippa said 10 percent on facilities. Yvette said the Trust requires the contingency to be shown as a separate line and cannot be spent without its written consent.

6. Budget

6.1 Yvette tabled the draft budget. Totals (pounds): scanners hire 19,800; operator posts (2 digitisation assistants, 6 months at 2,350 per month each) 28,200; conservation 31,200; mould specialist 4,200; storage server and backup 24,000; catalogue software and transcription module 22,500; hosting 31,800; facilities total 105,100 (the four items in 5.1 that Colm costed); furniture and computers 14,000; project manager (Aisha, 0.4 of her time for 8 months) 17,600; contingency 10,510. The grand total is 308,910 pounds.
6.2 Yvette noted that the total is 122,910 pounds higher than the grant of 186,000 pounds. Philippa said she has had a verbal assurance of up to 50,000 pounds from the county but nothing in writing, and Dr Hale has told her the Friends can pledge 20,000 pounds. That still leaves 52,910 pounds with no source. The group agreed it cannot sign the Trust agreement while this gap is open. Action on Philippa to get written confirmation from the county and to bring proposals for the remaining gap to the next meeting; Yvette to see which lines can be cut or phased.
6.3 Godfrey asked whether the 14,000 pounds for furniture and computers was inside the facilities figure of 105,100. Colm said no, it is separate.

7. Reporting to the Heritage Trust and communications

7.1 Yvette said the Trust asks for a half way report and the group agreed it should be submitted by 26 March 2027, once the reading room has opened, so that it can show real progress and trigger the second instalment of 74,400 pounds. The final report is due 30 June 2027.
7.2 The first instalment of 74,400 pounds will arrive only after the agreement is signed (see 6.2). Colm and Aisha pointed out that the climate unit order of 48,000 pounds on 20 October would have to be paid from county funds, because the grant money will not have arrived. Yvette will ask whether the county can underwrite this. If not, the order cannot be placed on 20 October and item 8.1 of the risks below applies.
7.3 Godfrey will draft a short notice for readers about the move and the closure. It cannot be published until the closure dates are decided (see 5.3). He suggested a monthly newsletter from December.
7.4 Philippa will ask the local paper whether it would run a piece when the first parish registers go online. Target for the first online release: 31 March 2027, with the 1813 to 1837 registers first.

8. Risks discussed

8.1 Climate unit delay: if the order is placed after 20 October the reading room date moves by the same number of weeks.
8.2 Staff: Aisha is the only person who knows the scanning workflow. Philippa wants a deputy named by 30 November.
8.3 Volunteer numbers: transcription depends on them and none are signed up yet.
8.4 Hosting terms: see 3.6.
8.5 Mould found in more than 12 boxes, which would delay the rolls.
8.6 The records have to be insured while they are moved, and Yvette has not yet asked the insurer.

9. Any other business

9.1 Rhiannon reported that 41 people responded to the call for volunteers. A training evening is being planned for the first week of December.
9.2 Dr Hale sent a note before the meeting asking that the Friends are told about the closure dates at least eight weeks ahead.
9.3 The next meeting is Wednesday 11 November at 10:00 in the Annexe.

Summary of actions agreed in the meeting
- Colm: confirm the sprinkler quote is firm and order the climate unit by 20 October.
- Aisha: file naming rules to Bram by 20 November; costed options for the throughput shortfall for the next meeting.
- Tomasz: finish the condition survey of the remaining 272 volumes by the end of November.
- Yvette: check with the Trust whether hosting can be prepaid; ask the insurer about the move; ask whether the county can underwrite the climate unit order; see which budget lines can be cut or phased.
- Philippa: written confirmation of county funds and proposals for the remaining 52,910 pound gap; talk to the Friends about the closure; name a deputy for Aisha by 30 November.
- Rhiannon: first volunteer training evening in the first week of December.

Je travaille au support de la Ligue des Quatre Vallées (football et futsal amateur) et j'ai neuf tickets ouverts ce matin que je n'ai pas le temps de traiter. Peux-tu rédiger pour chacun une réponse complète, polie et précise, adaptée à la personne et à sa situation, avec les prochaines étapes claires ? Si une information manque pour répondre sérieusement, dis-le-moi avant la réponse et propose la question à poser au demandeur.

Rappel des règles en vigueur cette saison (extraits du règlement intérieur, saison 2026-2027) :
- Les licences se prennent sur le portail de la Ligue. Tarifs : 38 euros pour un joueur de moins de 12 ans, 52 euros de 12 à 17 ans, 74 euros pour un adulte, 20 euros pour un dirigeant ou bénévole non joueur. Paiement par carte ou en trois fois sans frais jusqu'au 30 septembre.
- Une licence est validée quand trois éléments sont réunis : le paiement, le certificat médical ou le questionnaire de santé (selon l'âge), et la photo d'identité. Délai normal de validation : cinq jours ouvrés après réception du dernier élément.
- Un joueur ne peut pas être aligné sans licence validée. Un match joué avec un joueur non licencié est perdu par pénalité (0-3) et l'équipe paie une amende de 60 euros.
- Un changement de club (mutation) doit être demandé avant le 31 juillet pour une mutation normale. Après cette date, seule une mutation exceptionnelle est possible, avec un dossier justifié (déménagement, fermeture du club, etc.), traité en quinze jours.
- Un match peut être reporté seulement si les deux clubs sont d'accord et si la demande est déposée sur le portail au moins sept jours avant la date, sauf cas de force majeure (terrain impraticable décidé par la mairie, deuil, accident grave).
- Les remboursements de licence sont possibles avant la validation, ou après une blessure grave attestée par un certificat, au prorata des mois restants. Pas de remboursement pour un simple abandon.
- Les réclamations sur la feuille de match doivent être envoyées dans les 72 heures par le président du club ou son délégué.
- Un arbitre peut être récusé par un club seulement pour un motif écrit (lien de parenté, conflit déclaré), au moins dix jours avant le match. Le désignateur de la Ligue répond sous cinq jours ouvrés.
- Un club qui déclare forfait moins de 48 heures avant un match paie 80 euros d'amende, et 40 euros s'il prévient au-delà de ce délai ; trois forfaits dans la saison entraînent l'exclusion de l'équipe du championnat.
- Pour les mineurs, l'autorisation parentale est incluse dans le formulaire de licence ; sans elle, la licence reste en attente.

Informations du dossier : l'arbitre du match est désigné par le désignateur de la Ligue ; aucune plainte précédente à son sujet. Le match de coupe est prévu dans vingt et un jours. La feuille de match de l'équipe B indique que l'équipe a joué à sept contre neuf et que le match a été terminé, sans abandon. Le règlement prévoit qu'une équipe doit aligner au moins huit joueurs au coup d'envoi pour un match à onze, sinon le match est perdu par forfait (0-3) et l'amende de 40 euros s'applique si le club a prévenu plus de 48 heures avant, 80 euros sinon. Le club n'a pas prévenu la Ligue.
