Here is the design doc for our new turnaround tracking service at Halvorsen Ground Handling. I'm presenting it to the architecture group on Thursday and I would like a hard critique of it first: what is weak, what is missing, what could fail at the airport in real life. Please also propose at least two alternative designs for the parts you think are wrong, say which you would choose and why, and then give me a phased implementation plan with estimates, dependencies and what we should not build yet.

TECHNICAL DESIGN: TURNAROUND TRACKER (TT)
Author: Mirela Santoro-Eze. Reviewers: Anders Okwuosa, Beatrix Lindahl-Moreau. Status: draft 3.

1. Background

Halvorsen Ground Handling serves 11 airlines at Caldmoor Airport, with an average of 142 aircraft turnarounds a day in summer and 96 in winter. A turnaround is everything that happens between an aircraft arriving at a stand and leaving it again: chocks, passenger bridge or steps, unloading bags, cargo, cleaning, catering, fuelling, water and toilet service, loading, pushback. At present each task is recorded on paper by the team leader, and typed into a spreadsheet by the planning desk after the flight has left. This has three problems: delays are discovered late, our airline customers dispute delay codes because the times are written from memory, and the planning desk cannot see in real time which crews are free.

2. Goals

G1. Record the start and end of every turnaround task in real time, with the person who did it, from a handheld device.
G2. Show the operations control room a live board of all stands, with each aircraft's progress and an early warning if the turnaround is going to miss its scheduled off-block time (STD).
G3. Produce, for each flight, a delay report with the cause code, in the format required by our airline contracts, within 15 minutes of off-block.
G4. Allocate crews to tasks automatically, based on the schedule, qualifications and where each crew is.

Non-goals: payroll, fuel billing, baggage reconciliation (the baggage system stays as it is), and any change to the airport's own flight information system.

3. Constraints

- The apron has patchy Wi-Fi. Our measurements last winter show 7 percent of the apron is a dead zone, mainly behind Stands 14 to 17 and near the de-icing pad.
- Devices: 120 rugged handhelds (Android, 5 inch screens, gloves in winter). Team leaders carry one per team. There are 31 teams on a peak shift.
- Data from the airport: a flight schedule feed (arrivals, departures, stand, aircraft type, estimated times) sent as messages every time anything changes, about 40 messages per minute at peak.
- The airline contracts require 99.5 percent availability of the delay report data per month and keeping records for 5 years.
- The IT team is four engineers. Budget approved for development: 9 months, including testing.

4. Proposed architecture

TT is composed of the following parts:

4.1 Handheld app. A native Android app. The team leader taps one of the task buttons for the aircraft on their stand (for example "Bridge on", "Bags off started", "Bags off done"). Each tap creates an event with a timestamp from the handheld clock, the stand, the flight number, the task code and the user id. Events are saved in a local database on the handheld and sent to the server when a connection is available.

4.2 Event API. An HTTP service that receives events from the handhelds and writes them to a PostgreSQL database. It checks the user's token, rejects events from unknown devices, and returns the list of events it has stored. One server, two instances behind a load balancer.

4.3 Schedule ingest. A service that reads the flight schedule feed from the airport and updates the "flights" table. When a message arrives it overwrites the row for that flight. Estimated times are replaced by the newest estimate.

4.4 Progress engine. Every 30 seconds a job reads all open flights and all their events, and computes for each flight: which tasks are done, which are late relative to a standard timeline for the aircraft type, and the predicted off-block time. The result is written to a "flight_status" table.

4.5 Control room board. A web page that reads "flight_status" every 5 seconds and shows one row per stand, with colour: green, amber (predicted to leave up to 5 minutes late), red (more than 5 minutes late). The page is shown on four screens in the control room.

4.6 Delay report. A nightly job generates a PDF per delayed flight from the events and the cause code the team leader picked, and emails it to the airline's operations address. A planner can edit the cause code before 06:00.

4.7 Crew allocation. A rule-based assignment: when a flight is within 90 minutes of arrival, the system picks the team for the flight by matching aircraft type qualification and choosing the team whose previous task ended earliest. The planner can overrule. The plan is pushed to the handhelds as a list of flights for the shift.

5. Data model (outline)

- flights(id, number, aircraft_type, stand, sta, std, eta, etd, status)
- events(id, flight_id, task_code, kind [start|end], device_time, server_time, user_id)
- teams(id, name, shift, qualifications[])
- assignments(id, flight_id, team_id, planned_start)
- flight_status(flight_id, predicted_offblock, state, late_tasks[])
- delay_reports(flight_id, cause_code, edited_by, pdf_url, sent_at)

6. Failure handling

- If a handheld is offline, events are stored locally and sent later. The server keeps events in the order of device_time.
- If the event API is down, handhelds retry every 60 seconds.
- If the schedule feed is down, the board shows the last known data with a banner "Schedule feed interrupted".
- The database is backed up each night. In case of a failure we restore the last backup.
- If a team leader taps the wrong button, the only fix is to ask the planning desk, who change the record the next morning.
- If two handhelds send the same event twice (for example after a retry), the server stores both.

7. Security

- Each handheld logs in with the team leader's badge number and a four digit PIN. The token is valid for 12 hours.
- All traffic uses TLS. The control room board has no login because it is only on the internal network.
- Cause codes can be edited by planners only.
- Handhelds are managed devices: a lost device can be wiped from the office, and the app stores no personal data other than the user id.
- The event table is append-only. A correction is a new event that refers to the one it replaces, so the history of what was tapped and when is never lost.
- The database and the backup are in the airport's own data room. Backups are kept for 35 days and a restore has not yet been tested.

8. Rollout

Phase 1 (months 1 to 3): build the handheld app, event API and database. Phase 2 (months 4 to 6): schedule ingest, progress engine and board. Phase 3 (months 7 to 9): delay report and crew allocation. Pilot with one airline (Skyward Nordic, 14 flights a day) in month 8 and full rollout in month 9, in the first week of April.

9. Sizing and load

- A turnaround has about 12 recorded tasks, each with a start and an end, so about 24 events per flight. At 142 flights a day that is about 3,400 events a day, and at most perhaps 60 events a minute in the busiest 15 minutes of the morning bank. Schedule messages add 40 a minute at peak.
- Open flights at any moment: about 40 at peak. The progress engine therefore reads 40 flights and about 500 events every 30 seconds.
- Retention: 5 years of events is about 6.2 million rows (3,400 x 365 x 5), plus the PDF reports, around 300 KB each for about 20 percent of flights, which is roughly 15 GB over five years.
- Handhelds: 120 devices, of which about 62 are in use on a peak shift (31 teams, one handheld for the team leader and one spare per team).
- The control room board is the only component with a latency target: a tap on a handheld must show on the board within 10 seconds when the handheld has a connection.

10. Standard timeline (narrow-body example)

The progress engine compares actual events with a standard timeline for each aircraft type. For a typical narrow-body aircraft with 45 minutes scheduled on stand, in minutes after on-block (chocks on):

| Task | Planned start | Planned end |
|---|---|---|
| Chocks on, bridge or steps on | 0 | 3 |
| Bags and cargo off | 4 | 18 |
| Cleaning | 5 | 20 |
| Catering | 8 | 25 |
| Fuelling | 10 | 28 |
| Water and toilet service | 12 | 22 |
| Bags and cargo on | 22 | 36 |
| Boarding (airline, shown for reference) | 24 | 40 |
| Bridge off, doors closed | 40 | 42 |
| Pushback ready, chocks off | 42 | 45 |

For the prediction of off-block, the author proposes to take the latest planned end among tasks not yet done, plus the gap that task normally has before off-block, and add the average overrun of that task for that aircraft type over the last 30 days.

11. Testing and acceptance

- Unit tests for the progress engine using recorded days of events from the spreadsheet (we have 14 months).
- A replay tool that sends a recorded day of schedule messages and handheld events at 20 times speed.
- A field test on three stands for two weeks with a paper backup in place, comparing the times typed in by the planning desk with the times in the system. Acceptance: for 95 percent of tasks the two agree within 2 minutes.
- Acceptance for the delay report: the airline's operations manager signs off 30 consecutive flights.
- A test where the Wi-Fi is disconnected for 20 minutes on a stand in the dead zone, and all events appear on the server afterwards in the right order.

12. Delay cause codes and the delay report

- Each airline contract uses its own list of delay causes, but 80 percent of delay minutes fall into a few groups: late arriving aircraft, late bags or cargo, late fuel, late catering, late cleaning, crew not available, equipment not available, passenger or airline-caused (late boarding, late paperwork), and weather. The team leader picks one primary cause on the handheld at pushback, and may add a second.
- The report for a delayed flight shows: scheduled and actual on-block and off-block, the timeline of each task with actual start and end, the primary and secondary cause, the minutes of delay attributed to us and to others, and free text from the team leader (up to 300 characters).
- Today Skyward Nordic and two other airlines dispute about 6 percent of the delay codes we send. The goal of G3 is to cut disputes by half in the first six months.
- The report is signed in the system by the planner who edited it, if any; edits are logged with the old value, new value, user and time.

13. Open questions

- What is the standard timeline per aircraft type? We have it for 6 of the 14 types.
- Who owns the delay cause codes taxonomy, which differs between airlines?
- Should team leaders be able to correct an event after it has been sent?
- Do we need to store handheld GPS positions? The unions have not been asked.

14. Estimates and risks (author's view)

Team: 4 engineers for 9 months, no dedicated tester. Main risk: the airline contract requires 99.5 percent availability for delay report data, and we have no standby server. Second risk: clock differences between handhelds, which have shown up to 4 minutes of drift in our spot checks. Third: the planning desk may not trust automatic crew allocation. The author thinks the biggest technical risk is the prediction of off-block time.

Effort estimate by component (engineer-months, author's numbers):

| Component | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Handheld app (offline storage, sync, UI) | 8 |
| Event API and database | 3 |
| Schedule ingest | 3 |
| Progress engine and prediction | 6 |
| Control room board | 3 |
| Delay report and cause code editing | 4 |
| Crew allocation | 5 |
| Testing, replay tool and field trials | 2 |
| Deployment, monitoring and training | 2 |
| **Total** | **36** |

Four engineers for nine months is also 36 engineer-months, so the plan has no slack for illness, holidays, or the open questions in section 13.

# Larkfield Veterinary Clinic: Scheduling and Patient Records System (LVC-SRS)
Version 0.9, owner: Marguerite Oyelaran (practice manager), technical lead: Tobias Wennerström

## 1. Purpose and scope

Larkfield Veterinary Clinic has three consulting rooms, one surgical theatre, a small laboratory and a dispensary, served by four vets (Dr. Anselm Kowalczyk, Dr. Priya Raghunathan, Dr. Imogen Fairweather, Dr. Daniel Okonkwo-Lyle), five nurses and three reception staff. Today appointments live in a paper diary and a shared spreadsheet, and patient histories are split between index cards and a legacy database. LVC-SRS replaces all of this with one web application used on the reception desktop, the consulting-room tablets and the nurses' phones.

In scope: appointment booking, reminders, patient and owner records, clinical notes, medication dispensing, stock control for the dispensary, laboratory result intake, invoicing and daily takings. Out of scope for version 1: online payment, the owners' mobile app, and insurance claim submission.

## 2. Users and roles

| Role | Can do |
|---|---|
| Receptionist | Create and edit owners and patients, book and move appointments, take payment, print invoices. Cannot read clinical notes. |
| Nurse | Read and add clinical notes in "nursing" category, record weights and vitals, dispense stock against a prescription, enter lab results. Cannot sign prescriptions. |
| Vet | Everything a nurse can, plus sign prescriptions, close consultations, edit any clinical note written under their own name, and view the full history. |
| Practice manager | Everything except clinical notes, plus reports, price lists, user administration and stock adjustments above 5 units. |

Every user logs in with an individual account. Passwords must be at least 12 characters. After 10 minutes of inactivity the session locks; after 5 consecutive failed logins the account is locked for 15 minutes. All writes are recorded in an audit log (user, time, record, old value, new value) that cannot be edited from the application.

## 3. Owners and patients

3.1 An owner record has: surname, given name, at least one phone number, email (optional), postal address, preferred contact method (phone, email, none), and a free-text note. Duplicate detection: if a new owner has the same surname and the same phone number as an existing one, the system warns the user and offers to open the existing record. It does not block creation.

3.2 A patient belongs to exactly one owner at a time. Fields: name, species (dog, cat, rabbit, guinea pig, bird, reptile, other), breed (free text), sex (male, female), neutered (yes/no), date of birth (exact or estimated to the month), colour, microchip number (15 digits, optional), insurance reference (optional), and status (active, deceased, transferred). Marking a patient deceased cancels all future appointments and reminders for that patient and requires a vet.

3.3 Ownership transfer: a vet or the practice manager can move a patient to a different owner. The old owner stays in the history of the patient. Open invoices stay with the owner who was responsible when they were created.

3.4 Microchip numbers are unique across active patients. Entering a number already in use shows the patient it belongs to and refuses to save.

3.5 Weight is recorded in kilograms with one decimal for animals under 10 kg and with no decimal above. A weight that differs by more than 20 percent from the previous weight within 30 days is accepted but flagged for the vet.

## 4. Appointments

4.1 Appointment types and default lengths:

| Type | Default length | Room |
|---|---|---|
| Consultation | 15 min | Consulting room |
| Vaccination | 10 min | Consulting room |
| Dental check | 20 min | Consulting room |
| Surgery | 60 min | Theatre |
| Nurse clinic | 20 min | Consulting room |
| Lab drop-off | 5 min | None |

4.2 The diary shows one column per vet and one per room, in 5-minute slots, between the clinic opening hours: Monday to Friday 08:00 to 18:30, Saturday 09:00 to 13:00, closed Sunday and on the public holidays listed by the practice manager. Booking outside opening hours is refused.

4.3 A booking needs a patient, a type, a vet (or "any available vet"), a start time and a reason. The system rejects a booking if the vet, or the room, is already occupied for any part of the interval. A surgery booking additionally reserves a 30-minute recovery block directly after it in the theatre column, which cannot be booked by anyone else.

4.4 "Any available vet" chooses the vet with the fewest booked minutes on that day who is not on leave. Ties are broken alphabetically by surname.

4.5 Leave: the practice manager enters leave for a vet as a date range. Existing appointments inside the range are listed and must each be moved or cancelled before the leave is saved.

4.6 Moving an appointment keeps its history. Cancelling requires a reason from a list (owner request, no show, clinic cancelled, patient deceased, other). If an appointment is cancelled less than 2 hours before its start, the system adds a "late cancellation" mark to the owner. Three marks in 12 months show a banner at booking time. The banner does not block booking.

4.7 Emergency walk-ins can be added at the top of the day with a type of "Emergency" and no start time. They are shown in a separate queue and ordered by arrival. A vet picks one from the queue, and it then becomes a normal 30-minute appointment starting now, which may overlap the vet's next booking. The system warns of the overlap and lists the affected appointments.

4.8 Overbooking: a receptionist cannot overbook. The practice manager can, by confirming a warning that names the overlapped appointment. Overbooked entries are shown with a red border.

## 5. Reminders

5.1 Vaccination reminders are generated from the vaccination schedule on the patient. For each vaccine the vet sets an interval in months (for most vaccines 12, for some 36). A reminder is created 30 days before the due date and a second one 7 days before, unless a booking for a vaccination already exists.

5.2 Appointment reminders: 48 hours and 3 hours before the start, by the owner's preferred method. If the preferred method is "none", no reminder is sent. If the preferred method is email but no email is stored, the system falls back to phone text message and records that it did.

5.3 An owner can reply "C" to a text message to cancel. This cancels the appointment with the reason "owner request" and sends a confirmation. Any other reply is stored on the owner record and shown to reception.

5.4 Reminders are not sent between 21:00 and 07:30 local time; they are queued and sent at 07:30. A reminder for an appointment starting before 09:00 is sent the evening before at 20:00 instead of the 3-hour reminder.

## 6. Clinical notes and prescriptions

6.1 A consultation has: reason, history, examination findings, diagnosis, plan, and attachments (images or PDF up to 10 MB each, at most 8 per consultation). Notes are saved as a draft every 30 seconds. A consultation is closed by a vet; after closing, notes can only be extended through an addendum that carries its own author and timestamp.

6.2 A prescription lists drug, strength, form, dose per administration, frequency, duration in days, and total quantity. The total quantity must equal dose times frequency times days, within rounding to the pack unit; otherwise the system shows the calculated figure and asks the vet to confirm.

6.3 Controlled drugs (list maintained by the practice manager) require a second sign-off by another vet before they can be dispensed. The same person cannot give both sign-offs.

6.4 Allergy check: each patient can have allergies recorded. Prescribing a drug whose active ingredient matches a recorded allergy shows a blocking warning that the vet can override only by entering a reason.

6.5 Dose guidance: for drugs with a weight-based range in the formulary, a dose outside the range for the last recorded weight shows a warning. The weight must be less than 90 days old; otherwise the warning says the weight is out of date.

## 7. Dispensary and stock

7.1 Each stock item has a code, name, form, pack size, unit, reorder level, reorder quantity, supplier, cost price and sale price, and one or more batches with a batch number and expiry date.

7.2 Dispensing deducts from the batch with the earliest expiry that has enough quantity. A batch past its expiry date can never be dispensed. A batch expiring within 30 days is dispensed only if no later batch exists, and the nurse sees a notice.

7.3 When the total quantity of an item falls to or below its reorder level, it is added to the next morning's reorder list at 07:00. Items already on an open order are not added again.

7.4 Goods in: a nurse or the practice manager enters a delivery note against an order, one line per item and batch. Receiving more than was ordered is allowed with a warning; receiving an item that was not on the order is refused.

7.5 Stock adjustments (breakage, expiry write-off, count correction) require a reason. Adjustments above 5 units need the practice manager.

## 8. Laboratory

8.1 Samples are registered with the patient, a test panel and the collection time. The analyser sends results as a file dropped into a shared folder every few minutes. The system matches each result to a sample by the sample barcode.

8.2 A result outside the reference range for the species is marked high or low. A result more than three times outside range is marked critical and appears on the vet's home screen until acknowledged.

8.3 A result that cannot be matched to any sample goes into an "unmatched" list for the practice manager. Results are never discarded.

## 9. Invoicing and takings

9.1 An invoice is created automatically when a consultation is closed and collects the consultation fee, procedures and dispensed items from that visit. Prices are taken from the price list valid on the day of the visit. Sales tax is 20 percent on medicines, food and all services.

9.2 A receptionist can apply a discount of up to 10 percent; larger discounts need the practice manager. Payment methods: cash, card, and account (invoice sent to the owner, due in 30 days).

9.3 Invoices cannot be deleted. A mistake is corrected by a credit note that references the original and a new invoice.

9.4 End of day: the practice manager runs the daily takings report, which must reconcile totals by payment method with the sum of the day's invoices and credit notes. A difference blocks the day from being marked closed.

## 10. Non-functional requirements

10.1 Any screen loads in under 2 seconds on the clinic network with up to 12 users working at once. The diary for one day with 60 appointments loads in under 1 second.

10.2 All data is backed up nightly at 02:00 and the backup is restored and checked once a month. Loss of at most 24 hours of work is acceptable.

10.3 The application works in the two most recent releases of the browsers used on the clinic machines. The consulting-room tablets are used in landscape orientation only.

10.4 Personal data of owners is kept for 7 years after the last visit and is then anonymised. An owner can request an export of their data, which the practice manager produces as a PDF within 30 days.

10.5 Times are shown in the clinic's local time zone. The change to and from summer time must not move or duplicate any appointment.

## 11. Reports

11.1 The practice manager can run these reports for any date range of up to 366 days, as a screen table and as a CSV download: appointments by vet and type, cancellations and no shows by reason, revenue by category (consultations, procedures, medicines, food, other), revenue by vet, stock value by supplier, and expiring batches within 60 days.

11.2 The no-show report lists every owner with two or more no shows in the range, the dates, and whether a late cancellation mark was also added. The report counts a no show only when the appointment status is "no show"; a cancellation made after the start time is stored as a no show automatically.

11.3 Vets can see their own list of consultations that were opened but not closed for more than 24 hours. The list is shown on the vet's home screen with the oldest first. A consultation left open for more than 7 days is also listed for the practice manager.

11.4 Report figures must agree with the invoices: the revenue total of any report for a given range must equal the sum of invoices minus credit notes dated inside that range, to the penny.

## 12. Migration from the old system

12.1 Before go-live, owners, patients and the last five years of consultations are imported from the legacy database through a one-off import tool. The tool reads a CSV export for each of the three entity types and writes a log with one line per rejected row.

12.2 A row is rejected when a required field is empty, when a patient refers to an owner that does not exist in the import, or when a microchip number is already used by an active patient. Rejected rows do not stop the import; accepted rows are saved.

12.3 Imported consultations are stored as closed, with the author "Legacy import" and the original date. They cannot be edited, only extended with an addendum.

12.4 The import can be run again on the same files without creating duplicates: an owner is identified by the legacy id, which is stored on the new record.

12.5 On the last working day before go-live the diary is frozen; the paper diary is used for emergencies only, and those entries are typed into the new system within 24 hours of go-live.

# Jardín Botánico de Valdeflores
## Informe trimestral de gestión: tercer trimestre de 2026 (julio a septiembre)
Elaborado por la dirección técnica para el patronato. Fecha de cierre: 3 de octubre de 2026.

### 1. Resumen ejecutivo

El tercer trimestre ha sido el más complejo del año por la combinación de una ola de calor en julio, la reapertura del invernadero de montaña y el inicio de las obras del nuevo sistema de riego. Recibimos 41.860 visitantes, un 6,2 % más que en el mismo trimestre de 2025 (39.410), aunque un 3,1 % menos de lo previsto en el presupuesto, que contaba con 43.200. Los ingresos totales fueron de 512.400 euros frente a unos gastos de 538.900, de modo que el déficit del trimestre es de 26.500 euros y el déficit acumulado del año asciende a 41.300 euros. La subvención autonómica de 90.000 euros se cobró íntegra en septiembre, por lo que la tesorería a 30 de septiembre es holgada: 187.600 euros.

Los tres hechos que más pesan en la valoración del trimestre son: la pérdida de 212 ejemplares de la colección de helechos arborescentes durante la ola de calor, el éxito del programa escolar (9.870 alumnos, un récord) y el retraso de seis semanas en las obras de riego, que obliga a revisar el calendario de la segunda fase.

### 2. Visitantes y ventas

| Mes | Visitantes 2026 | Visitantes 2025 | Previsión presupuesto |
|---|---|---|---|
| Julio | 12.640 | 12.980 | 14.100 |
| Agosto | 14.920 | 13.350 | 15.300 |
| Septiembre | 14.300 | 13.080 | 13.800 |
| Total | 41.860 | 39.410 | 43.200 |

La caída de julio respecto del año anterior (un 2,6 %) se debe sobre todo a los siete días de cierre parcial por calor extremo, en los que solo se abrió el parque entre las 8:00 y las 12:30. En agosto se recuperó con las noches de apertura nocturna "Jardín a la luz de la luna", que atrajeron a 2.150 personas en seis fechas con una media de 358 por noche. Septiembre superó la previsión por primera vez en el año gracias a los grupos escolares.

Reparto por tipo de entrada: general 44 %, reducida (jubilados, estudiantes, familias numerosas) 17 %, abono anual 8 %, grupos escolares 24 % y entradas gratuitas (menores de 6 años, personal acompañante) 7 %. El precio medio por visitante fue de 8,94 euros, frente a 8,71 en el tercer trimestre de 2025. Las ventas anticipadas por internet representaron el 34 % de las entradas de pago, ocho puntos más que hace un año. Se cerraron 3 incidencias de la pasarela de pago, de las cuales una (el 19 de agosto, de 2 horas y 40 minutos) provocó colas en taquilla y quejas en redes.

### 3. Ingresos y gastos

El gasto en agua fue un 38 % superior al previsto (22.800 euros frente a 16.500) por el riego de emergencia de julio, y la energía se mantuvo en línea con el presupuesto.

### 4. Colecciones y conservación

El herbario recibió 318 nuevos pliegos y se digitalizaron 1.240, con lo que el total digitalizado alcanza el 64 % de los 41.000 pliegos. El banco de semillas amplió su catálogo con 57 accesiones, entre ellas 11 especies amenazadas de la sierra de Altozano; las pruebas de germinación realizadas en septiembre dieron un 82 % de éxito de media, por encima del objetivo del 75 %.

En las colecciones vivas, la ola de calor del 9 al 18 de julio, con máximas de 41 grados, causó la pérdida de 212 ejemplares de la colección de helechos arborescentes (el 31 % del total de 684). La causa principal fue el fallo de dos de las cuatro bombas de nebulización del umbráculo, que quedaron fuera de servicio durante 36 horas. Se han replantado 90 ejemplares procedentes del vivero propio y se han encargado 60 más a un jardín socio. Está pendiente determinar la compensación del seguro, cuya franquicia es de 8.000 euros.

El invernadero de montaña reabrió el 22 de julio después de once meses de reforma. Alberga 143 especies de flora de alta montaña con un control de temperatura que, según los registros de agosto, se mantuvo dentro de un grado de la consigna el 96 % del tiempo.

### 5. Educación y programas públicos

El programa escolar atendió a 9.870 alumnos de 212 centros, frente a 7.640 alumnos del tercer trimestre de 2025. La cifra incluye las visitas de septiembre, que concentraron el 71 % del total. Se impartieron 388 talleres con una ocupación media del 87 %. La encuesta a los docentes (214 respuestas) dio una valoración media de 4,6 sobre 5; el aspecto peor valorado fue el tiempo disponible para el almuerzo (3,4).

Entre los programas públicos destacan los 24 paseos guiados de fin de semana (media de 31 asistentes), el ciclo de conferencias "Plantas y clima" (cuatro sesiones, 410 asistentes en total) y el programa de voluntariado, que cuenta con 86 voluntarios activos, 14 más que en junio. Las horas de voluntariado del trimestre fueron 2.930.

### 6. Obras e infraestructura

La primera fase del nuevo sistema de riego (sectores A a D, 11 hectáreas) comenzó el 1 de julio con una duración prevista de 10 semanas. Una veta de roca no detectada en el estudio geotécnico obligó a modificar el trazado de la tubería principal en el sector C, lo que añadió seis semanas. La primera fase terminará previsiblemente el 21 de octubre, en lugar del 9 de septiembre. El sobrecoste estimado es de 38.000 euros sobre un contrato de 412.000, cantidad que aún no ha sido aprobada por el patronato. La segunda fase (sectores E a H) estaba prevista para enero y no puede empezar antes de marzo, ya que la época de brotación de las colecciones de primavera no admite zanjas abiertas.

Otras actuaciones: sustitución de las dos bombas de nebulización averiadas (14.600 euros, pagadas en septiembre, imputadas a obras e inversiones menores), repintado de la verja norte y reparación del camino del arboreto, cerrado durante tres semanas por un desprendimiento.

### 7. Tienda y vivero

La tienda y el vivero facturaron 48.700 euros, un 11 % más que en el tercer trimestre de 2025, con un margen bruto de 17.500 euros (36 %). Los productos más vendidos fueron las plantas aromáticas del vivero (4.120 unidades), las semillas de la colección de flora autóctona (2.870 sobres) y la línea de cuadernos ilustrados con láminas del herbario. La pérdida de la responsable de tienda en agosto se cubrió con una persona del equipo de taquilla, pero el inventario de septiembre mostró diferencias de 1.340 euros en la zona de papelería, que se están investigando. El vivero propio produjo 6.300 plantas, de las cuales 90 se destinaron a reponer los helechos; esto redujo en unas 400 unidades la disponibilidad para la venta pública.

Dos propuestas están sobre la mesa: abrir una tienda en línea limitada a semillas y papelería, con un coste estimado de puesta en marcha de 9.500 euros, y ampliar el horario del vivero los sábados por la tarde. Ninguna se ha presupuestado aún.

### 8. Comunicación y redes

El gasto en comunicación fue de 19.400 euros, un 8 % menos que el presupuestado (21.100). La campaña "Jardín a la luz de la luna" supuso 6.800 euros y generó el 78 % de las menciones del trimestre en redes sociales. La web recibió 168.000 visitas (un 14 % más que en el trimestre anterior) y el boletín cuenta con 11.240 suscriptores, con una tasa de apertura del 41 %. La incidencia de la pasarela de pago del 19 de agosto produjo 63 comentarios negativos en redes, y se respondió a todos en menos de 24 horas. La valoración media en el principal portal de opiniones es de 4,5 sobre 5 con 1.380 opiniones, frente a 4,6 en junio.

El servicio de prensa organizó dos visitas para periodistas, una dedicada a la pérdida de los helechos y otra a la reapertura del invernadero de montaña. La cobertura de la reapertura fue positiva en seis medios locales y uno regional.

### 9. Personal y seguridad

La plantilla es de 41 personas (36 equivalentes a jornada completa). Hubo dos bajas voluntarias, un jardinero y la responsable de tienda, y una incorporación temporal de verano de cuatro monitores para los talleres. La rotación anual de la plantilla fija es del 9,8 %. Se registraron 5 accidentes laborales leves (3 cortes, 1 picadura con reacción alérgica, 1 torcedura) y ninguno con baja superior a siete días. Los 19 trabajadores de campo completaron la formación sobre golpe de calor antes del 31 de julio, pero la formación se hizo después de la primera semana de la ola de calor.

Entre los visitantes hubo 17 incidencias de primeros auxilios, 11 de ellas por calor o mareos, y ninguna grave. El desfibrilador de la entrada principal se revisó en agosto.

### 10. Riesgos y previsión para el cuarto trimestre

Riesgos principales: el nuevo retraso de las obras (que puede extenderse si las lluvias de otoño anegan la zanja del sector C), la caída previsible de visitantes en noviembre, la compensación del seguro por los helechos y el aumento de precios de la energía a partir de diciembre. Para el cuarto trimestre se prevén 22.500 visitantes, ingresos de 238.000 euros y gastos de 251.000 euros, con lo que el déficit anual se situaría en unos 54.300 euros, dentro del margen de 60.000 euros aprobado por el patronato en diciembre del año pasado.

### 11. Decisiones que se piden al patronato

1. Aprobar el sobrecoste de 38.000 euros de la primera fase de riego.
2. Autorizar el aplazamiento de la segunda fase a marzo de 2027.
3. Decidir si se contrata un seguro específico para la colección de helechos arborescentes.
4. Aprobar un plan de contingencia por calor extremo con cierre parcial automático a partir de 38 grados.
5. Ratificar el calendario de actividades de otoño, que incluye la fiesta de la castaña del 7 y 8 de noviembre.

```sql
    status            VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL,   -- OPEN, UNDER_REVIEW, APPROVED, DENIED, CLOSED
    cause_code        VARCHAR(12),
    description       TEXT,
    amount_claimed    NUMERIC(12,2),
    amount_approved   NUMERIC(12,2)
);

CREATE TABLE claim_note (
    note_id           SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    claim_id          INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES claim(claim_id),

    claim_id          INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES claim(claim_id),

);

CREATE TABLE claim_status_history (
    history_id        SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    claim_id          INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES claim(claim_id),

    new_status        VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL,

    changed_by        INTEGER REFERENCES adjuster(adjuster_id)
);

CREATE TABLE cause_code (
    cause_code        VARCHAR(12) PRIMARY KEY,
    product_code      VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
    label             VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE claim_reserve (
    reserve_id        SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    claim_id          INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES claim(claim_id),
    set_on            DATE NOT NULL,
    reserve_amount    NUMERIC(12,2) NOT NULL,
    set_by            INTEGER REFERENCES adjuster(adjuster_id)
);

CREATE TABLE claim_document (
    document_id       SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    claim_id          INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES claim(claim_id),
    doc_type          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,   -- PHOTO, INVOICE, REPORT, LETTER
    file_name         VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    uploaded_at       TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now(),
    size_bytes        BIGINT
);

CREATE TABLE fraud_flag (
    flag_id           SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    claim_id          INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES claim(claim_id),
    raised_on         DATE NOT NULL,
    rule_name         VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    score             INTEGER NOT NULL,
    reviewed          BOOLEAN DEFAULT false
);

-- Indexes that exist today
```

Some facts about the data, as of the first of October: policyholder has about 410,000 rows, policy about 560,000, claim about 1.9 million (of which roughly 4 percent are OPEN or UNDER_REVIEW), claim_note about 7.5 million, payment about 3.1 million and claim_status_history about 6.2 million. claim_reserve holds about 2.4 million rows (a claim usually has one to three reserve changes), claim_document about 5.8 million, and fraud_flag about 140,000, of which roughly a third are not yet reviewed. About 8 percent of claims have no adjuster yet because they sit in the intake queue. Payments marked reversed are bounced transfers or cancelled cheques, about 1.5 percent of all rows. Month-end reports run on the read replica, which has 16 GB of memory and a spinning-disk array.

```sql
-- Q1: month-end paid total by product for September 2026 (runs 4+ minutes)
SELECT p.product_code,
       SUM(pay.amount) AS paid_total
FROM payment pay, claim c, policy p
WHERE pay.claim_id = c.claim_id
  AND c.policy_id = p.policy_id
  AND to_char(pay.paid_on, 'YYYY-MM') = '2026-09'
GROUP BY p.product_code
ORDER BY paid_total DESC;

-- Q2: open claims older than 60 days, with adjuster name (runs 90 seconds)
SELECT c.claim_number,
       c.reported_at,
       (SELECT a.full_name FROM adjuster a WHERE a.adjuster_id = c.adjuster_id) AS adjuster,
       now() - c.reported_at AS age
FROM claim c
WHERE c.status IN ('OPEN', 'UNDER_REVIEW')
  AND c.reported_at < now() - interval '60 days'
  AND c.claim_id NOT IN (SELECT claim_id FROM claim_status_history WHERE new_status = 'APPROVED')
ORDER BY c.reported_at;

-- Q3: average days to close, per adjuster, for claims closed in the last 12 months
SELECT a.full_name,
       COUNT(*) AS closed_claims,
       AVG(DATE_PART('day', c.closed_at - c.reported_at)) AS avg_days_to_close
FROM claim c
JOIN adjuster a ON a.adjuster_id = c.adjuster_id
WHERE c.closed_at > now() - interval '12 months'
  AND c.status = 'CLOSED'
GROUP BY a.full_name
HAVING COUNT(*) > 0
ORDER BY avg_days_to_close;

-- Q4: policyholders with three or more claims in the last 24 months
SELECT ph.full_name, ph.postcode, COUNT(c.claim_id) AS claims
FROM policyholder ph
JOIN policy p ON p.policyholder_id = ph.policyholder_id
JOIN claim c ON c.policy_id = p.policy_id
WHERE c.loss_date >= current_date - 730
GROUP BY ph.full_name, ph.postcode
HAVING COUNT(c.claim_id) >= 3
ORDER BY claims DESC;

-- Q5: claims where total paid exceeds the approved amount
SELECT c.claim_number, c.amount_approved,
       (SELECT SUM(amount) FROM payment WHERE claim_id = c.claim_id) AS total_paid
FROM claim c
WHERE c.amount_approved IS NOT NULL
  AND (SELECT SUM(amount) FROM payment WHERE claim_id = c.claim_id) > c.amount_approved;

-- Q6: latest reserve per open claim, compared with what has been paid so far
SELECT c.claim_number,
       r.reserve_amount,
       COALESCE(pd.paid, 0) AS paid_so_far,
       r.reserve_amount - COALESCE(pd.paid, 0) AS remaining
FROM claim c
JOIN claim_reserve r ON r.claim_id = c.claim_id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT claim_id, SUM(amount) AS paid FROM payment GROUP BY claim_id) pd
       ON pd.claim_id = c.claim_id
WHERE c.status IN ('OPEN', 'UNDER_REVIEW')
  AND r.set_on = (SELECT MAX(set_on) FROM claim_reserve WHERE claim_id = c.claim_id)
ORDER BY remaining DESC;

-- Q7: unreviewed fraud flags with a score of 70 or more, with the number of documents
SELECT f.flag_id, c.claim_number, f.rule_name, f.score,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM claim_document d WHERE d.claim_id = c.claim_id) AS documents
FROM fraud_flag f
JOIN claim c ON c.claim_id = f.claim_id
WHERE f.reviewed = false
  AND f.score >= 70
  AND c.status <> 'DENIED'
ORDER BY f.score DESC, f.raised_on;
```

# The Night Lift

## 1.

At ten past five in the morning the snow is still the colour of slate, and Ines Marchetti is already standing at the bottom station of the Kestrel chair with a thermos in one hand and a wrench in the other, listening to the cable. She has done this every working morning for eleven winters. The sound she is waiting for is not a sound exactly. It is the absence of one particular note, a thin sort of whine that the main sheave makes when the bearing is going, and which she has never once been able to describe to anyone who has not heard it.

Today there is no whine. There is only the long low breath of the motor turning over with nobody on the line, and below it, from the car park, the first diesel of the day: Gustavo, the groomer, taking his machine up the Gentian run to finish the corduroy before the lifts open.

She puts the wrench down on the rail, unscrews the thermos, and drinks. The coffee is too sweet. Her daughter filled it last night as a favour and has never learned that Ines takes it black. She drinks it anyway.

The resort of Kestrel Hollow has four lifts, nineteen runs, a hotel with a name nobody uses, and a population of two hundred and six in winter, which swells to something over four thousand on the weekends if the snow report is kind. It sits in a bowl of rock that the guidebooks call "sheltered" and the locals call "the sink," because everything that falls on the surrounding peaks eventually comes down to it, whether it is snow, or weather, or rumour. Ines grew up three valleys east and came here at twenty-six for a season, to get away from a man, and stayed because the lift needed someone who would not skip the morning check.

Her daughter, Lucía, is sixteen and sleeps through all of this. She lives in the small flat above the ski store with the window that looks out on the Hollow, and she has her own opinions about the mountain, most of which are unfavourable. She wants to go to the city for school and then, she says, never come back. Ines has not told her that this is exactly what she once said herself, in a kitchen three valleys east, to a mother who had said nothing at all and simply poured the tea.

By six she has walked the whole length of the bottom terminal. She has checked the safety gate, the emergency stop, the loading carpet, the grip tester, and the little brass plaque with the name of the engineer who commissioned the lift, a man who died before she was born and whom she thinks of, without any sentiment, as a colleague. She signs the log. The log says, in her handwriting, in the column where other people write "nothing to report," *Nothing to report.* She has never been able to bring herself to write it any other way, even on the mornings when it is not quite true.

At seven the others arrive. Teodor comes first, nineteen and long-limbed, with the lanyard of the seasonal staff still new enough to be stiff. Then Marguerite from the ticket office, who tells Ines every morning, in the same words, that the roads were awful, and then Dag, the patrol leader, who says nothing and goes straight to the radio.

"Wind at the top?" Ines asks him.

"Twelve. Gusting twenty-five." He does not look up from the handset. "We open the upper section at nine if it holds."

"It won't hold."

"Then we open at ten," says Dag, and that is the whole of the morning meeting.

## 2.

The first thing that goes wrong is small. At a quarter to nine, with the lower section already running and a line of about forty people shuffling toward the carpet in their bright jackets, the third chair from the end of the loading zone sticks on its grip. It does not fall. It does not even slow. It simply fails to release the cable cleanly, so that for the length of one breath the whole carrier tilts, a small grey animal shrugging its shoulder, and then it rights itself and goes on up the hill with two teenagers in it who have not noticed anything at all.

Ines notices. She is already moving before she has decided to, down the loading ramp, one hand on the stop button and her eyes on the cable. She does not press it. She has pressed it exactly four times in eleven years, and each time she has been right, and each time she has spent the following week explaining herself to the insurers. She watches the next chair come around and puts her hand on the grip as it passes, as a doctor lays two fingers on a wrist, and feels it: a drag, a stickiness, like a drawer that has swollen in damp weather.

"Teodor," she says. "Take the carpet."

"I've only done it once on my own."

"Then this is the second time."

She goes into the machine room and finds the grease gun, and then, because she is the kind of person who checks the thing she does not want to be true, she goes back out and counts the chairs. There are seventy-two on the line. She walks the length of the lower station and puts a hand on the grip of every seventh one as it comes by. By the time she has done ten she has found three that drag.

It is the grease, she thinks. A batch of it from the new supplier, which Per in the workshop swore was the same specification as the old, and which she had signed for without testing, for the first time in her life, because it was the last week of November and everyone was tired.

She radios Dag. "I'm going to close the Kestrel for an hour. Maybe two."

There is a silence on the channel that she knows well. It is the silence of a man doing arithmetic with money. The Kestrel is the only chair that reaches the top terminal, and the top terminal is where the hotel's guests are waiting for the one run that matters, the long Gentian, which today has the best snow in the valley.

"Do you need to?" says Dag finally.

"I think so."

"Think, or know?"

"Dag," she says. "If you want me to know, I will have to let one fail."

Another silence. Then: "Close it. I'll tell reception."

She presses the stop button. The line shudders and halts, forty chairs hanging in the cold, and from the queue at the bottom comes a long ragged groan, the sound of a crowd that has just been told something it has already guessed. She does not turn around to look at them.

While they are working, Valentina Brask comes down from the hotel. She is the manager, a tall woman in a long camel coat who has run the place for four winters and still wears city shoes on the mountain, and she walks along the cordon tape with the unhurried air of someone who has already decided what she is going to say.

"I have sixty guests who booked the week for the Gentian," she says. "Two of them are on the phone to their travel agent as we speak."

"I know."

"Is it something you can fix?"

"It's something I am fixing," says Ines, and keeps her eyes on the grip she is cleaning. "If you want it quicker, there is no way to make it quicker. If you want it safe, this is the way."

Valentina is quiet for a moment. The wind lifts the hem of her coat and lets it fall. "The last manager," she says, "would have had you running by ten, on the grounds that the chairs were going round anyway."

"The last manager was a fool."

"Yes," says Valentina. "That is more or less why he is the last one." She looks at the line of grey chairs, the bright cold air, the mountain going up behind them into cloud, and something in her shoulders gives way, only a little. "Tell me when it is ready. I will tell the guests it is a precaution. It will be a precaution, won't it?"

"It is a precaution today," says Ines.

Valentina catches the word that has not been said, the *today*, and takes it back up the hill with her, and does not mention it again.

It takes her and Per and Teodor an hour and fifty minutes to flush and re-grease the grips on every carrier, working down the line in the lee of the terminal with the wind pulling at their sleeves. The grease from the new supplier is the colour of butter, and when she rubs a little of it between her fingers it feels wrong, a fine grit under the smoothness, like sugar stirred into a paste. She puts a sample in a jar and writes the date on the lid.

At eleven fifty the lift is running again, and by noon the line has doubled. Nobody thanks her. A man in a red jacket mutters something about a "pointless delay" to his wife as he passes, and Ines, who has heard worse in three languages, lifts her thermos to him and smiles.

## 3.

That evening, after the last skier has been swept off the Gentian and the lights along the lower slope have gone out one by one, Ines is still in the machine room with the jar on the bench in front of her. The room smells of oil and hot metal and the faint sweetness of the coffee she has not finished. Outside, the wind has finally dropped. She can hear, through the thin wall, the tick of the cooling motor.

She has a phone number for the supplier and a mobile number for their sales representative, a young man called Ruben Aalto who visited in October with a box of free gloves and a very good-looking brochure. She calls the first and gets a recorded message in a language that is not quite the one she is expecting. She calls the second and he answers on the sixth ring, cheerful, with the noise of a restaurant behind him.

"Ines! How is the mountain?"

"There is grit in your grease."

A pause. The restaurant noise recedes, as though he has walked into a corridor. "Grit," he says.

"I have it in a jar. I can send you a photo. Three of the carriers were dragging this morning, and I closed my lift for two hours on a Saturday with a full house."

"That is, I mean, I am really sorry about that. But those batches are all tested, I can assure you."

"I'm sure they are," says Ines. "I'm also sure that I am looking at them."

When the call ends she sits for a while with her elbows on the bench. It is not a disaster, she knows that. A grip that drags can be cleaned. A chair that tilts for a breath is not a chair that falls. But she has spent eleven winters learning to tell the difference between a thing that has gone wrong and a thing that is about to, and the part of her that does this has been awake since a quarter to nine, saying very quietly: this is the second.

The first was in March, though she had not counted it then. A bolt on the upper station, an inspection hatch that someone had closed without the second latch. She had found it at six in the morning and fixed it in a minute and written *Nothing to report* in the log. She had not wanted a fuss. She had not wanted to be the woman who made the engineers drive up from the city for a latch.

She takes the log from the shelf and opens it to March, and there, under the fourteenth, is her own handwriting, neat and wrong. She reads it three times. Then she turns to today's page, and for the first time in eleven years, in the column where she writes the sentence she is proudest of, she writes something else.

*Grips dragging on 11 carriers. Lift closed 08:50 to 11:50. Grease from new supplier has grit in it; sample retained in the workshop, labelled. Also: inspection hatch, upper station, 14 March, second latch missing. Should have reported. I am reporting it now.*

She looks at it for a long time. Then she signs it, and at the bottom, on a line of its own, she adds the time.

Per comes in as she is closing the log, smelling of the workshop, a stocky man of sixty with a cap he wears indoors and out. He puts a half-empty tin on the bench beside the jar, turns it so the label faces her, and taps the batch number with a thick finger.

"Four tins left in the store," he says. "Same batch. I have taped them shut."

"You didn't have to stay."

"I signed for the delivery too," says Per. "You are not the only one in this building who does not like the taste of being wrong." He studies the jar, then her face. "The old supplier is still in business. I can ring them in the morning."

"Ring them," says Ines. "And ask them what they charge to be right."

"They will say too much."

"It will still be cheaper than the alternative," she says, and Per, who has never in her hearing agreed with anything aloud, nods once and takes his cap off, as one does at a small funeral.

When she steps outside, Teodor is sitting on the steps of the terminal with his boots off and his socks steaming in the cold, looking up at the sky, which has cleared. There are more stars than she remembers from last winter. Behind him the Kestrel chairs hang motionless, a long string of them rising into the dark, and the snow beneath them has taken on a blue colour she has never found a word for in any of her three languages.

"Is it bad?" he says.

"No." She sits down next to him on the step, which is freezing through her trousers. "It's the kind of thing that is only bad if you pretend it isn't."

He thinks about this with the seriousness of nineteen. "Is that a rule?"

"It's about the only one I've got."

Down in the village a dog starts barking, and then another, and from somewhere behind the hotel she hears the engine of Gustavo's machine starting up for the night shift on the Gentian, its lights swinging across the slope like a slow lighthouse. Ines finishes the last of her coffee, which has gone cold and is still too sweet, and finds that she does not mind it.

"Tomorrow," she says, "you can do the carpet again. All morning."

"On my own?"

"With me standing right behind you," she says. "Which is how everyone starts."

# Menu Simplification and Kitchen Performance in a Multi-Site Restaurant Group: A Cluster-Controlled Study

Authors: Rosalind Achterberg, Kofi Mbeki-Larsen, Teodora Vuković
Affiliation: Operations Research Unit, Tallowfield Hospitality Group

## 2. Methods

### 2.1 Setting

Tallowfield Hospitality Group operates 31 full-service restaurants in four regions of the same country, under three brands: Harbour Table (seafood and grills, 11 sites), Olive & Ember (Mediterranean, 12 sites) and The Copper Spoon (regional comfort food, 8 sites). All sites use the same point-of-sale system, the same inventory software and the same central purchasing contracts. Menus are set by brand, not by site, and contain between 54 and 71 items.

### 2.2 Design

We conducted a cluster-controlled study with the restaurant as the unit of allocation. Twenty-four sites were eligible: they had been open for at least 18 months, had a head chef in post for at least six months, and were not scheduled for refurbishment during the study. The remaining seven sites were excluded for these reasons (refurbishment, 3; new head chef, 2; seasonal opening only, 2).

The 24 eligible sites were formed into 12 pairs matched on brand, region and average weekly covers (within 15 percent). Within each pair, one site was assigned to the intervention and the other to control by a coin toss made by the first author in the presence of the regional directors. The study ran for 16 consecutive weeks from 5 May to 24 August 2026: a four-week baseline period in which all sites operated normally, followed by a 12-week intervention period. Sites were told the allocation at the end of the baseline period.

### 2.3 Intervention

Intervention sites reduced their menu by 30 percent. The reduction was made in three steps, each designed by the brand's executive chef together with the head chef of the site: (a) removal of the items with the lowest sales mix in the previous 12 months, subject to keeping at least four vegetarian main courses and at least one dish per allergen group; (b) a shared prep list in which any ingredient that appeared in at least three remaining dishes was prepared in batches twice a day, at 10:00 and 16:30, in quantities set from a simple forecast based on the same weekday in the previous four weeks; and (c) a weekly 30-minute meeting in which the head chef reviewed the waste log. Control sites kept their existing menus and prep routines. Both groups received the same training in waste logging.

### 2.4 Outcomes

The primary outcome was food waste, measured in kilograms per 100 covers. Secondary outcomes were: median ticket time (minutes from order to the kitchen marking the last dish as ready), food cost as a percentage of food sales, guest satisfaction (mean score on a five-point scale from the post-meal survey sent by email to guests who booked through the group's website), and staff overtime (hours per week per site, taken from payroll).

Covers per week and food sales were collected as secondary measures of demand, to check that any change was not caused by a loss of business.

### 2.5 Data collection

Food waste was weighed by kitchen staff at the end of every service. Staff used a calibrated scale to weigh three bins (preparation waste, spoilage and plate waste) and entered the weights on a tablet. Ticket times and covers were exported automatically from the point-of-sale system. Food cost used inventory counts taken every Monday. Guest satisfaction was collected for all bookings made through the website, which account for approximately 38 percent of covers. Payroll data were provided by the finance department.

### 2.6 Statistical analysis

We analysed data at the site-week level. For each outcome we fitted a linear mixed model with fixed effects for period (baseline or intervention), group (intervention or control) and their interaction, and random intercepts for site and for matched pair. The interaction coefficient is the difference-in-differences estimate and is reported with a 95 percent confidence interval. The analysis followed the intention-to-treat principle: all sites were analysed in the group to which they were allocated. We did not adjust for multiple comparisons, because the five secondary outcomes were considered to be of separate operational interest. The significance level was 0.05, two-sided. Analyses used R version 4.4.

The sample size was not calculated before the study; the number of pairs was set by the number of eligible sites. A post hoc calculation showed that 12 pairs give 80 percent power to detect a difference of 1.9 kg per 100 covers in the primary outcome, assuming a between-site standard deviation of 2.4.

### 2.7 Ethics and data handling

The study was an evaluation of an operational change within the company and was approved by the group's management board. Kitchen staff were informed of the study by their head chefs and were free to decline to take part in the end-of-study questionnaire, which was anonymous. Guest survey responses were stored without names or email addresses, and no guest could be identified from the data supplied to the authors. Payroll data were supplied as weekly totals per site, so no individual employee's hours were visible. No external funding was received; the cost of the additional training and of the auditors' travel, 18,400 euros in total, was met by the group's operations budget. The first and second authors are employees of the group and the third author is a regional operations manager for two of the participating regions.

## 3. Results

### 3.1 Flow of sites and data

All 24 sites completed the study. One intervention site (Harbour Table, coastal region) closed for 3 weeks in week 9 because of flooding; its data for those weeks are missing and were not imputed. A further two control sites introduced menu reductions of their own during the intervention period: one removed 6 items from week 10 after a supplier problem, and one removed 4 items from week 13 for seasonal reasons. Both were kept in the control group. In total the analysis includes 381 site-weeks and approximately 690,000 covers.

### 3.2 Baseline characteristics

| Characteristic | Intervention (n = 12) | Control (n = 12) |
|---|---|---|
| Harbour Table / Olive & Ember / Copper Spoon | 4 / 5 / 3 | 4 / 5 / 3 |
| Seats, mean | 112 | 109 |
| Covers per week, mean | 1,840 | 1,795 |
| Menu items, mean | 63 | 62 |
| Head chef tenure in months, median | 21 | 24 |
| Food waste, kg per 100 covers | 9.8 | 9.6 |
| Median ticket time, minutes | 21.4 | 21.1 |
| Food cost, % of food sales | 31.2 | 30.9 |
| Guest satisfaction, 1 to 5 | 4.21 | 4.19 |
| Staff overtime, hours per week | 14.6 | 14.2 |

The two groups were similar at baseline on all measured variables.

### 3.3 Primary outcome

Food waste in intervention sites fell from 9.8 to 7.1 kg per 100 covers (a change of -2.7), while control sites moved from 9.6 to 9.3 (a change of -0.3). The difference-in-differences estimate was -2.4 kg per 100 covers (95% CI -3.4 to -1.4; p < 0.001), which corresponds to a relative reduction of 24 percent against the intervention group's baseline. Of the three bins, the largest reduction was in preparation waste (-1.7 kg per 100 covers), followed by spoilage (-0.6) and plate waste (-0.1). The effect was visible from the second week of the intervention and did not grow after week 8.

In the intervention group, 11 of the 12 sites reduced waste; the site that did not was the flooded site, whose waste rose by 0.4. Excluding this site gave an estimate of -2.7 (95% CI -3.6 to -1.8).

### 3.4 Secondary outcomes

| Outcome | Intervention: baseline to intervention | Control: baseline to intervention | Difference-in-differences (95% CI) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Median ticket time, min | 21.4 to 18.2 | 21.1 to 20.9 | -3.0 (-4.1 to -1.9) |
| Food cost, % of sales | 31.2 to 29.4 | 30.9 to 30.7 | -1.6 (-2.5 to -0.7) |
| Guest satisfaction, 1 to 5 | 4.21 to 4.18 | 4.19 to 4.20 | -0.04 (-0.12 to 0.04) |
| Staff overtime, hours/week | 14.6 to 12.9 | 14.2 to 14.4 | -1.9 (-3.3 to -0.5) |
| Covers per week | 1,840 to 1,812 | 1,795 to 1,801 | -34 (-96 to 28) |
| Food sales per week, EUR | 41,300 to 41,050 | 40,100 to 40,250 | -400 (-1,650 to 850) |

Ticket times fell in all 12 intervention sites. The reduction in food cost was equal to approximately 650 euros per site per week at the intervention group's average sales. Satisfaction scores did not differ between the groups; 2,914 survey responses were received in the intervention group and 2,873 in the control group, a response rate of 11 percent in both. Free-text comments mentioning "choice" or "variety" rose from 3.1 percent to 5.6 percent of comments in intervention sites and were unchanged in control sites.

### 3.5 Sensitivity analyses

Excluding the two control sites that reduced their own menus raised the primary estimate to -2.6 (95% CI -3.6 to -1.6). Using only the final eight weeks of the intervention period gave -2.5 (95% CI -3.6 to -1.4). Including brand as a fixed effect did not change the estimates materially; the effect was largest for Olive & Ember (-3.1) and smallest for The Copper Spoon (-1.4), although the study was not designed to detect differences between brands. The intra-cluster correlation for the primary outcome was 0.46.

### 3.6 Implementation and fidelity

Intervention sites removed between 17 and 23 menu items (mean 19.0, a reduction of 30 percent of the mean baseline menu of 63 items). All 12 sites kept at least four vegetarian main courses. The twice-daily batch prep was followed on 91 percent of audited services (the head chefs' own logs; the regional operations managers audited 6 services per site in unannounced visits and found 88 percent). Attendance at the weekly waste meeting was 10.4 of 12 weeks on average; two sites held fewer than eight meetings. Sites that held at least ten meetings (n = 8) had larger reductions in waste than those that held fewer (-2.9 versus -2.0 kg per 100 covers), but this comparison was not planned and the groups were not formed at random.

The ten control sites that did not alter their menus also made no changes to their prep routines. At the start of week 10, one regional director reported that two control chefs had asked to copy the batch prep list from a neighbouring site; the request was refused.

### 3.7 Staff and guest feedback

At the end of the study a short questionnaire was sent to the 142 kitchen staff in the intervention sites; 97 replied (68 percent). Of these, 71 percent agreed or strongly agreed that the shorter menu made service calmer, 18 percent were neutral and 11 percent disagreed. Sixty-two percent said they would like to keep the shorter menu, and 24 percent said the menu was now too small. The head chefs reported that the main difficulty was the removal of dishes with loyal customers, and in four sites a regular dish was returned to the menu as a weekend special after week 6. These dishes were counted as part of the intervention menu.

No food-safety incidents were recorded in either group during the study period. One allergen-related complaint was received in a control site and none in an intervention site.

### 3.8 Data completeness

Waste weights were missing for 2.1 percent of services in the intervention group and 3.4 percent in the control group, mostly because of tablet failures; missing services were not imputed and the weekly totals were scaled to the number of services recorded. Ticket times were complete. Payroll and inventory data were complete for all site-weeks except those of the flooded site. Survey responses were received for 11 percent of web bookings in both groups.

## sync-to-shore.sh

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Sends new data files to the shore server over the satellite link.
# Run from cron every 30 minutes while at sea.

DATA_DIR=/mnt/datastore
SHORE=ops@shore.skerrywren.example.org
LOG=/var/log/sync.log
LOCK=/tmp/sync.lock

if [ -f $LOCK ]; then
    echo "already running" >> $LOG
    exit 0
fi
touch $LOCK

cd $DATA_DIR

# Is the link up?
ping -c 1 shore.skerrywren.example.org > /dev/null
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
    echo "$(date) link down" >> $LOG
    exit 1
fi

for cruise in $(ls); do
    echo "$(date) syncing $cruise" >> $LOG
    rsync -avz --partial --bwlimit=0 $cruise $SHORE:/srv/incoming/ >> $LOG 2>&1
    if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
        find $cruise -name "*.raw" -mtime +2 -exec rm {} \;
    fi
done

rm $LOCK
echo "$(date) done" >> $LOG
```

## Some context

The vessel has about 40 days at sea per cruise and a satellite link that runs at roughly 256 kbit/s shared with the crew's welfare internet, which is why there is a limit on the bandwidth that data transfer may use when the link is busy. The datastore is a 12 TB RAID volume, mounted at /mnt/datastore, with one directory per cruise (named like WREN-2026-04). The raw files from the CTD rosette are small but the multibeam echosounder writes around 40 GB a day, and the science party insists that nothing is deleted from the ship until the chief scientist, Dr. Ximena Abernathy-Osei, has confirmed that the shore copy is complete. The ingest container is also reachable by the scientists' laptops through the ship's network, and the ship's IT officer, Bartholomew Nkemelu, has told me that the guest wifi is on the same network segment as the instruments, which I know is not ideal.

Two things happened on the last cruise that I want to make sure cannot happen again. On day 23 the datastore reached 94 percent and the nightly script deleted the oldest cruise directory on the volume, which turned out to be WREN-2026-02, whose shore copy had stopped half way through three weeks earlier without anyone noticing. Then on day 31 the CTD stopped sampling for about eleven hours overnight because the serial adapter had reset, and the watchdog restarted the container over and over without fixing it, so the gap was only found when the morning shift looked at the plots. The Prometheus alert for that case never fired. Please assume the scientists will want any change to be easy to explain to a non-specialist, and that I can edit files on the ship but cannot easily pull new images while at sea.

Below is our quarterly operations review for the Harrowgate Glassworks furnace and finishing site. I have to present it to the board on Thursday and I have not had time to read it properly. Please give me a section-by-section summary, then a list of the recommendations you would make to the board, ordered by how urgent they are.
