HARROWGATE GLASSWORKS LTD
Quarterly Operations Review, Q3 (July to September)
Prepared by: Marit Oyelaran, Head of Operations
Circulated to: Board of Directors, Site Leadership Team
Status: Final draft for board meeting

1. Executive summary

The third quarter was the first full quarter with Furnace 2 running on the new oxy-fuel burner package, and the results are mixed. Output of saleable glass rose to 4,310 tonnes against a plan of 4,150 tonnes, a gain of 3.9 percent. Natural gas use per tonne of melted glass fell by 11.2 percent compared with the same quarter last year, which is better than the 8 percent we promised the board in March. Against that, our overall yield from melt to shipped product slipped from 81.4 percent to 79.8 percent, mostly because of a bad six weeks in the annealing lehr at the finishing hall. Customer returns rose in the month of August and one large order of laboratory bottles for Pellam Scientific was rejected in full. Two reportable injuries occurred, both minor. The quarter ended with a cash position that is healthy, but the planned cold repair of Furnace 1 now looks like it cannot be delayed past next autumn.

2. Production and yield

Furnace 1 (the older end-port regenerative furnace) produced 1,880 tonnes of saleable glass, 6 percent under plan, because it ran at reduced pull from 12 July to 2 August while the crown was monitored after a hot spot was found on the north side. Furnace 2 produced 2,430 tonnes, 12 percent over plan. Its pull rate averaged 71 tonnes per day against a design figure of 68.

Yield loss by cause, as a share of all glass melted:

- Forming rejects (wall thickness, cords, seeds): 8.9 percent
- Annealing breakage and stress rejects: 6.4 percent
- Packing and handling breakage: 2.1 percent
- Customer returns credited back: 1.3 percent
- Cullet that could not be recycled because of contamination: 1.5 percent

The annealing figure is the main concern. Lehr 3 in the finishing hall had two failed heating zones between 20 July and 28 August. The maintenance log shows that the zone controller was replaced on 21 July, but the replacement part was the wrong rating and tripped twice. The correct part arrived on 30 August. During those weeks the line was run at lower speed with a flatter temperature profile, which cut throughput by about 14 percent and produced a visible rise in stress rejects, particularly on thick-walled jars.

3. Energy and emissions

The oxy-fuel package on Furnace 2 cut gas use to 3.46 gigajoules per tonne melted, down from 3.90 a year ago. Electricity use rose by 0.21 gigajoules per tonne because of the on-site oxygen plant, so the net energy saving is smaller than the gas figure suggests. We estimate the net saving at 7.6 percent. Carbon dioxide from combustion fell by 9.8 percent per tonne. Nitrogen oxides at the stack are the open issue: the monthly average on Furnace 2 was 780 milligrams per cubic metre in July, 910 in August and 840 in September. Our permit limit is 1,000 milligrams, but the regulator has told us informally that it expects new installations to hold below 800. The burner vendor, Calder Combustion, has proposed a staged-air adjustment that it says will bring the figure down by about 15 percent for a one-off fee of 38,000 pounds.

Furnace 1 remains on the old regenerative system and has not changed. Its nitrogen oxide level sits at around 1,150 milligrams per cubic metre under a derogation that expires in June of next year. This is a hard date and is discussed again under risks.

4. Quality and customers

Complaints rose from 19 in Q2 to 31 in Q3. The breakdown was 12 for chips and surface defects, 9 for dimensional problems, 6 for colour variation in amber glass, 3 for contamination (stones and unmelted batch) and 1 for wrong labelling. The single biggest event was the Pellam Scientific order of 62,000 laboratory bottles, shipped on 14 August and rejected on 3 September after the customer found cords in the neck finish that caused leaks under their vacuum test. We have agreed to replace the full lot at our cost, estimated at 118,000 pounds including freight and the lost slot on the line. Root cause work found that the bottles came from a period when the Furnace 1 forehearth temperature drifted by about 9 degrees because of the crown hot spot, and our inline inspection camera was set to a tolerance suited to the wider necks we normally make, so it did not catch them.

Colour variation in amber was traced to inconsistent addition of iron sulphide in the batch house during two weeks when the second batch operator was on leave. The batch scales have been recalibrated and a second sign-off added.

On the positive side, on-time delivery was 94.7 percent against a target of 93, and two new customers signed supply agreements, a regional brewer and a cosmetics packager.

5. Safety and people

There were two reportable injuries. The first was a cut to the hand of a packer on 9 August when a broken jar was handled without the correct glove. The second was a sprained ankle at the cullet yard on 22 September on an uneven surface after rain. Lost time totalled 11 days. The rolling twelve-month injury rate is 3.1 per million hours worked, down from 3.8. Safety training for the three new furnace operators was completed on schedule. Staff turnover in the quarter was 4.2 percent annualised, but we lost our only qualified lehr technician to a competitor in October, and the role is currently covered by an agency contractor at roughly twice the cost.

An employee survey in September had a 71 percent response rate. Scores on safety culture were high at 4.3 out of 5. Scores on communication from management were low at 3.0, with night-shift comments most frequently asking for earlier notice about schedule changes.

6. Maintenance and capital projects

The Furnace 2 oxy-fuel project closed out at 2.96 million pounds against a budget of 3.10 million, which is under budget by 4.5 percent. The lehr 3 controller upgrade is now a priority. The compressed-air system leak survey found 23 leaks, estimated to waste 6 percent of compressor output, and 17 are fixed. The new inline inspection camera for the narrow-neck line was ordered on 18 September at a price of 164,000 pounds with delivery in January.

The cold repair of Furnace 1 is the largest item. A full rebuild of the regenerators and a partial crown replacement is estimated at 6.4 million pounds with a ten-week shutdown. Engineers from the refractory supplier inspected the crown in July and said it could probably run another twelve months with careful monitoring but gave no guarantee. We should plan the shutdown for the quieter trading period in January to March of the year after next, or sooner if the crown deteriorates.

7. Raw materials and cullet

Batch materials were supplied without interruption. Soda ash cost rose 7 percent in August under the annual price clause, and sand cost was flat. The supplier of our high-purity sand, Tilbury Quarry Products, delivered 14 loads with iron content above the agreed limit of 0.015 percent, which forced us to add more decolourising agent in clear glass and raised the batch cost per tonne by about 1.40 pounds on those days. We have issued a formal notice and asked for a credit of 9,300 pounds. The supplier has promised a response by the end of October and has offered to install a second sieving stage at its own plant.

Cullet is the most useful raw material we have, because every 10 percent of cullet in the batch saves roughly 2.5 percent of melting energy. The average cullet ratio on Furnace 2 was 38 percent and on Furnace 1 it was 31 percent. External cullet from the bottle bank contract was 2,900 tonnes in the quarter, but 1.5 percent of everything melted had to be rejected because of ceramics, metal caps and heat-resistant glass mixed in. We trialled a new optical sorter on the incoming cullet line in September on a hire basis. It removed 82 percent of the ceramic and stone pieces that previously got through. Purchase of a permanent unit is quoted at 410,000 pounds, and the payback from reduced contamination and a higher cullet ratio is estimated at about three years.

8. Product segments and customers

Revenue and volume by segment, with the change against the same quarter last year:

| Segment | Tonnes shipped | Revenue (GBP m) | Change in revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| Food and drink containers | 2,460 | 5.92 | +5.1% |
| Laboratory and pharmaceutical | 640 | 2.71 | -3.4% |
| Cosmetics and perfumery | 520 | 1.84 | +12.8% |
| Decorative and tableware | 390 | 1.04 | +1.9% |
| Specialty and architectural | 300 | 0.33 | -8.0% |

The decline in the laboratory segment is directly connected to the Pellam rejection and one other customer pausing orders while it audits our complaint handling. The cosmetics segment grew fastest and has the best margin, at about 19 percent against 9 percent for food and drink. The architectural segment is small and has been loss-making for two years because short runs require frequent colour changes on Furnace 2. We recommend that the board decide in the Q4 meeting whether to continue it.

Our five largest customers account for 58 percent of revenue, down from 63 percent a year ago. The biggest single customer, a national brewery group, accounts for 17 percent and its contract is due for renewal in March. Its buyer has indicated that price will be the main topic and has asked for a recycled-content commitment of at least 60 percent by weight, which our current cullet ratios on Furnace 1 would not support.

9. Follow-up on Q2 actions

At the last review the Site Leadership Team agreed six actions. Their status is as follows.

1. Complete the Furnace 2 oxy-fuel commissioning. Done on 12 July.
2. Reduce complaint response time to under five working days. Partly done. The average fell from 9.1 to 6.4 working days, but the Pellam case took 12 days to receive a first formal answer.
3. Introduce a second sign-off on batch weighing. Done in September, after the amber problem showed it was needed.
4. Agree a rebuild plan for Furnace 1 with the refractory supplier. Open. A proposal was received but a firm cost and schedule are not yet agreed.
5. Replace the forklift fleet's gas trucks with electric units. Delayed. Two of six trucks have been delivered because the charging points were not installed in time.
6. Roll out the improved shift handover form. Done on all shifts, though night shift compliance is only 70 percent.

10. Finance

Revenue for the quarter was 11.84 million pounds against a plan of 11.30 million. Operating profit was 1.37 million, or 11.6 percent of revenue, below last year's 12.4 percent because of the Pellam provision of 118,000 pounds and higher agency labour costs. Gas prices were stable under our fixed contract until March. Cash at quarter end was 4.2 million pounds, with no drawn debt. A reserve of 1.5 million has been earmarked from retained profit for the Furnace 1 rebuild, which leaves a large gap that would have to be financed.

11. Risks

The main risks recorded this quarter are:

1. Furnace 1 crown failure before a planned shutdown. A failure would stop about 45 percent of output for an estimated twelve to sixteen weeks. Likelihood is rated medium, impact severe.
2. Expiry of the nitrogen oxide derogation on Furnace 1 in June. If the rebuild has not begun, we would need to install abatement equipment, which has been quoted at 1.9 million pounds, or reduce its output.
3. Loss of skilled staff in annealing and forming. Only one person in the company is fully trained on lehr control.
4. Quality escapes from the narrow-neck line until the new camera arrives.
5. Rising electricity prices, because the oxygen plant has made Furnace 2 more exposed to power costs.

12. Outlook for Q4

We expect output of about 4,200 tonnes. The staged-air adjustment would be done during the planned two-day maintenance stop in November if approved. We will complete the leak repairs, hire a permanent lehr technician, and run a trial of tighter inline inspection settings manually until the camera is installed. The board is asked to consider the Furnace 1 rebuild timing and financing at its next meeting.

13. Decisions requested from the board

The Site Leadership Team asks the board to take the following decisions at its next meeting.

1. Approve the 38,000 pound staged-air adjustment on Furnace 2.
2. Approve purchase of the permanent optical cullet sorter at 410,000 pounds, subject to a final quotation.
3. Give direction on the timing of the Furnace 1 rebuild and authorise the finance director to open talks with lenders for the gap above the 1.5 million reserve.
4. Decide whether to continue the architectural glass segment.
5. Approve a retention payment for the lehr technician role and the cost of a trainee to build depth of skill.

Marit Oyelaran
Head of Operations

These are the notes from our planning meeting at the dairy on Tuesday. Nobody agreed who would write the plan up, so it is me. Can you turn them into a full project plan for the new maturing cellar and the cheese-on-demand launch, with workstreams, owners, dates, dependencies and a risk list? Where the notes are vague, flag it and suggest something sensible.

---

WETHERBY CROFT DAIRY
Meeting notes: Maturing Cellar and Direct Sales Planning
Date: Tuesday 8 October, 10:00 to 12:45
Location: Farm office, upstairs room
Present: Tamsin Ogunleye (managing director, chair), Bartholomew Rees (head cheesemaker), Ilse Brandvold (finance and administration), Kofi Ansah-Whitlock (milk supply and farm liaison), Perpetua Lindgren (sales and marketing), Desmond Achterberg (maintenance and building works)
Apologies: Yusuf Haldane (quality and food safety), who sent written comments that were read out
Notes taken by: Ilse Brandvold

1. Purpose of the meeting

Tamsin opened by saying that the dairy has outgrown its single maturing room. We now make about 41 tonnes of cheese a year, mostly the hard cloth-bound cheddar-style wheel and the smaller washed-rind round, and about a third of every batch has to be sold young because there is nowhere to keep it. Older cheese sells for between 40 and 60 percent more per kilo. Two other things came together this summer. The old cattle shed next to the dairy became free when the heifers moved to the north field, and the regional food board offered a grant for small producers who add storage and direct sales. The grant application closes on 29 November. The aim is to decide today what we will do, who does it and by when, so that the application can be written in time.

2. The maturing cellar

Desmond presented the survey of the old shed. It is a stone building 14 metres by 6 metres, with a sound roof and a concrete floor that slopes toward a drain on the east side. Walls are 55 centimetres thick, which gives good natural thermal mass. There is a three-phase power supply at the yard gate, 22 metres away, but the cable to the shed would need replacing. Water is present, but there is no hot water.

Bartholomew said that the shed could be divided into two rooms: a hard-cheese room at 11 to 13 degrees and 85 percent humidity, and a washed-rind room at 12 to 14 degrees and 92 percent humidity. He wants a small separate anteroom for brushing, turning and packing so that staff do not carry the smell and the moulds into the make room. He estimated the shed could hold 2,800 wheels of the large cheese on three-tier wooden racking or about 60 tonnes in total, which would let the dairy double production over four or five years.

Desmond gave a rough budget from two builders who visited:

- Floor resurfacing and drainage: 11,500 pounds
- Insulated internal partition walls and doors: 9,800 pounds
- Refrigeration and humidity control for two rooms: 31,000 pounds
- Electrical cable and distribution: 6,400 pounds
- Racking in spruce and stainless fittings: 14,000 pounds
- Anteroom fit-out with washable wall cladding and handwash basins: 8,300 pounds
- Contingency of 10 percent: 8,100 pounds

Total about 89,100 pounds. Ilse noted that these are verbal figures and nobody has given a written quote. Tamsin asked Desmond to get two written quotes for the refrigeration, since that is the largest item and the one most likely to be wrong. Desmond said refrigeration firms in the area are booked until January for installation but will send quotes within three weeks.

Discussion about whether to use a ground-source system for cooling. Bartholomew liked the idea because of stable temperatures, but Desmond said the cost would be at least double and the grant guidelines do not clearly cover it. Decision: go with conventional refrigeration, but design the plant room so that a heat pump could be added later.

3. Food safety and approval

Yusuf's written comments were read by Ilse. The local authority must approve any new maturing room before cheese is stored there for sale, and the process normally takes six to ten weeks after the inspector receives the final plans. He warned that the floor drainage must meet the standard for a food room, with a trapped gully and a sealed floor with coved edges, and that wooden racking is acceptable only if the supplier can confirm the wood is untreated and the dairy holds a written cleaning procedure for it. He asked for a pest control contract to be extended to the new building and for a new hazard analysis document, which he will write if he has the layout drawing by the end of November. He also said he is not comfortable with the washed-rind room sharing an air system with the hard cheese room, because of the risk of cross-contamination of surface cultures. Bartholomew agreed that each room needs its own evaporator and fan, and Desmond will add this to the quote request.

4. Direct sales and the cheese-on-demand idea

Perpetua presented the second part of the plan. Currently about 70 percent of the dairy's cheese goes through three wholesalers and 30 percent through the farm shop and two markets. Wholesale pays an average of 11.80 pounds per kilo, shop and markets 19.50. She proposed a subscription and mail-order service called Cheese Club, in which customers choose a monthly box of 1.2 kilos with a choice of cheese ages and receive a card from the cheesemaker. She believes 400 subscribers within 18 months is realistic, based on 1,100 names on the shop email list and a pilot of 35 boxes at the summer fair, of which 31 were bought again.

The proposed price is 34 pounds a box including delivery. Ilse worked out that, with packaging at about 3.60 pounds, courier at 6.20, and the cheese at an internal cost of 9.40 per box, the margin would be about 14.80 per box before staff time and website fees. At 400 subscribers that is about 71,000 pounds a year in gross margin. She asked whether the delivery cost is realistic for summer when cool packs are needed. Perpetua said she would test two couriers with chilled packaging over the next four weeks.

Kofi raised a point about milk. Doubling production would need roughly 480,000 litres more a year than the dairy takes now. The home herd and the two neighbouring farms that supply can give about 150,000 litres more. Kofi has spoken to a third farm, the Larkspur family, who may be able to supply 200,000 litres but only if the dairy agrees a price above the standard rate and accepts their milk twice a week rather than daily. The remaining volume would have to come later. Tamsin said that doubling in one step is not the plan, and that the first goal is to age more of what the dairy already makes.

5. Website and order system

Perpetua said the current shop website cannot take recurring payments. Two options were discussed: a hosted shop platform at about 70 pounds a month plus 2 percent fees, or having a freelance developer build a custom system. Everyone preferred the hosted platform. Perpetua will set up a test shop and report back. Ilse asked for the system to produce a daily pick list and courier labels automatically. Perpetua believes the platform can do this through an add-on at 19 pounds a month.

6. Staffing

Bartholomew said that with the second room, the dairy will need a full-time cellar person to turn, brush and wash cheeses. A candidate from the dairy college has been mentioned by his old teacher, but there is no job description yet. Tamsin asked Ilse to draft a job description with a salary range of 26,000 to 29,000 pounds. Perpetua said she needs a part-time packing and customer service person from March, for about 20 hours a week.

7. Funding

Ilse summarised funding. The grant could cover 40 percent of eligible costs up to 45,000 pounds, which is for the building and equipment but not for the website or staff. The dairy would need to fund the balance of the cellar of about 44,000 pounds. The business has 38,000 pounds in reserve and an overdraft facility of 25,000 pounds that is not currently used. The bank's small business manager has offered to talk about a five-year equipment loan at around 7.2 percent. Tamsin said she is not keen to use the overdraft for building work and would prefer a loan, with the reserve kept for working capital. Kofi asked about the price for extra milk and whether the grant allows that. Ilse said it does not, so the cost of milk will have to be funded from cash flow.

8. Timeline discussed

Tamsin wants the cellar in use before the spring flush of milk in April, because that is when there is most cheese to store. Working back from that:

- Grant application submitted by Friday 29 November
- Final plans to inspector by end of November
- Written quotes by Friday 1 November (refrigeration), 15 November (building)
- Start of building work as soon as the grant decision is known, expected in late January
- Refrigeration installation as soon as available, possibly February
- Inspector approval by end of March
- Cheese Club soft launch in May, public launch in September

Desmond doubted that the building could be finished by April if the grant decision slips. Nobody had a plan for this case. Tamsin said she would rather start the floor and drainage at the dairy's own risk in December than lose the season, provided the grant rules allow work that began before the decision. Ilse will find out.

9. Cheese quality, ageing plan and the product range

Bartholomew set out what he would do with the extra cellar space. The large cloth-bound wheel is currently sold at 5 to 6 months. He wants to hold half of each batch to 12 months and a smaller share to 18 months, which is the age at which it wins medals and fetches the highest price. The washed-rind round would move from 6 weeks to 10 weeks for part of each batch, and he wants to try a new smaller blue-veined cheese of about 1.5 kilos, which needs its own corner of the washed-rind room, since the blue mould spreads easily. He suggested a small trial of 40 wheels this winter in the existing make room fridge to see whether the dairy can control the mould. Yusuf's note said that any blue cheese must be kept physically separate and have its own tools, brushes and racking. Bartholomew accepted this and said the blue trial may have to wait until the anteroom exists.

The effect on cash flow was discussed. Holding cheese for 12 months instead of 5 means that money is tied up for longer. Ilse estimated that moving half of all production to 12 months would need an extra 31,000 pounds of working capital at its peak in the second year, since the cheese made in month one is not sold until month thirteen. Tamsin said this is the reason she wants to keep the reserve for working capital rather than build with it.

Perpetua asked that each wheel is labelled with the date of make so that Cheese Club customers can choose by age. She would like to start a small "vintage" range with numbered wheels. Bartholomew said he can do this with a stamped tag on the cloth.

10. Packaging, couriers and customer service

Perpetua reported on the first two courier quotes. Courier A charges 6.20 pounds for a next-day box under 2 kilos to most of the country and 9.10 to the Scottish islands and Northern Ireland. Courier B is 5.40 pounds but offers only two-day delivery on Mondays and Tuesdays to avoid weekend storage. She prefers next-day for cheese quality. Boxes would be shipped Monday to Wednesday only so that no parcel is in the network over a weekend. Packaging would be a recyclable cardboard box with a wool-fibre liner, and she has asked a supplier for samples. The wool liner costs more than foam, about 1.10 pounds extra, but customers in the summer pilot commented on it positively.

Ilse asked how many people would be needed to pack. Perpetua said that at 400 boxes a month, packing would take about 25 hours a week, more at Christmas, when the dairy could expect up to three times the volume. It was agreed that seasonal temporary help would be needed in December and that this must be in the cost plan. Tamsin asked about complaints and returns. Perpetua proposed a simple promise: if a box arrives late or warm, the dairy replaces it without discussion. She estimated a loss of about 2 percent of boxes.

11. Insurance, labelling and legal points

Ilse reminded the meeting that the dairy's insurance covers storage at the current site only. The new building must be added, along with cover for stock held at higher value because aged cheese is worth far more than young cheese. She will request a quote. Labelling for mail order also needs a closer look. Each box must list allergens, the use-by or best-before date and the dairy's approval number, and distance-selling rules mean the website must show a cancellation policy. Perpetua will check these with the trading standards officer, whom she knows from the market. Desmond noted that fire regulations for the new building should be checked, since two rooms with refrigeration plant and timber racking might need a fire alarm and extinguishers. Tamsin asked him to include these in the building quotes.

12. Other points

Yusuf also asked for a decision on the cheese-testing laboratory contract, which renews in January. The dairy pays 4,200 pounds a year, and a cheaper lab 40 kilometres away has quoted 3,500. Postponed. Kofi mentioned that the milk tanker route might change in the new year, and he will confirm the dates. The next meeting is on Tuesday 22 October at 10:00.

Actions recorded at the meeting (no dates given unless stated)

- Desmond: written quotes for refrigeration and building (dates above)
- Ilse: grant application, job description for cellar person, check start-before-decision rule
- Perpetua: courier tests, hosted shop test
- Kofi: talk to Larkspur farm about price and delivery pattern
- Bartholomew: layout drawing of the two rooms and anteroom
- Yusuf: hazard analysis once the drawing is ready

Here is the schema and the reporting queries for our mushroom farm's production database (PostgreSQL). The weekly report has become slow since we passed two years of data, and I suspect the design has other problems too. Please review the design, tell me which indexes I need and why, and rewrite the queries with an explanation of each change.

```sql
-- Fenwick Hollow Mushrooms: production tracking
-- PostgreSQL 15

CREATE TABLE species (
    species_id      SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    common_name     TEXT NOT NULL,
    latin_name      TEXT,
    colonise_days   INTEGER NOT NULL,
    fruit_days      INTEGER NOT NULL,
    target_temp_c   NUMERIC(4,1),
    target_humidity INTEGER
);

CREATE TABLE growing_rooms (
    room_id         SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    room_name       TEXT NOT NULL,
    capacity_blocks INTEGER NOT NULL,
    room_type       TEXT NOT NULL,   -- 'incubation' or 'fruiting'
    active          BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE
);

CREATE TABLE substrate_batches (
    batch_id        SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    mixed_on        DATE NOT NULL,
    recipe          TEXT NOT NULL,
    straw_kg        NUMERIC(8,2),
    sawdust_kg      NUMERIC(8,2),
    bran_kg         NUMERIC(8,2),
    sterilised      BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
    notes           TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE grow_blocks (
    block_id        SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    species_id      INTEGER REFERENCES species(species_id),
    batch_id        INTEGER REFERENCES substrate_batches(batch_id),
    room_id         INTEGER REFERENCES growing_rooms(room_id),
    inoculated_on   DATE NOT NULL,
    moved_to_fruit  DATE,
    discarded_on    DATE,
    discard_reason  TEXT,
    weight_kg       NUMERIC(5,2)
);

CREATE TABLE harvests (
    harvest_id      SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    block_id        INTEGER REFERENCES grow_blocks(block_id),
    harvested_at    TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    flush_number    INTEGER NOT NULL,
    weight_kg       NUMERIC(6,3) NOT NULL,
    grade           TEXT,            -- 'A', 'B', 'C'
    picker          TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id     SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_name   TEXT NOT NULL,
    customer_type   TEXT,            -- 'restaurant', 'market', 'wholesaler'
    city            TEXT,
    email           TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id        SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id     INTEGER REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    ordered_at      TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    delivery_date   DATE,
    status          TEXT DEFAULT 'open'
);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
    item_id         SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id        INTEGER REFERENCES orders(order_id),
    species_name    TEXT NOT NULL,
    grade           TEXT NOT NULL,
    kg              NUMERIC(6,2) NOT NULL,
    price_per_kg    NUMERIC(6,2) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE climate_readings (
    reading_id      BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    room_id         INTEGER REFERENCES growing_rooms(room_id),
    read_at         TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    temp_c          NUMERIC(4,1),
    humidity        INTEGER,
    co2_ppm         INTEGER
);

-- Sensors write one row per room every minute, so this table has grown
-- to roughly 11 million rows. Only the last 14 days are used by the app.

CREATE INDEX idx_harvests_block ON harvests(block_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id);

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Reports
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

-- 1. Weekly harvest by species and grade, last 8 weeks
SELECT s.common_name,
       h.grade,
       date_trunc('week', h.harvested_at) AS week,
       SUM(h.weight_kg) AS total_kg
FROM harvests h
JOIN grow_blocks b ON b.block_id = h.block_id
JOIN species s ON s.species_id = b.species_id
WHERE h.harvested_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '8 weeks'
GROUP BY s.common_name, h.grade, date_trunc('week', h.harvested_at)
ORDER BY week DESC, s.common_name, h.grade;

-- 2. Yield per block by species (biological efficiency, kg harvested per
--    kg of block weight), for blocks that are finished
SELECT b.block_id,
       s.common_name,
       b.weight_kg AS block_kg,
       (SELECT SUM(weight_kg) FROM harvests WHERE block_id = b.block_id) AS harvested_kg,
       (SELECT SUM(weight_kg) FROM harvests WHERE block_id = b.block_id) / b.weight_kg * 100 AS efficiency_pct
FROM grow_blocks b
JOIN species s ON s.species_id = b.species_id
WHERE b.discarded_on IS NOT NULL
   OR b.moved_to_fruit < CURRENT_DATE - 60;

-- 3. Contamination rate by substrate recipe
SELECT sb.recipe,
       COUNT(*) AS blocks,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE b.discard_reason ILIKE '%contam%') AS contaminated,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE b.discard_reason ILIKE '%contam%') * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 1) AS pct
FROM grow_blocks b
JOIN substrate_batches sb ON sb.batch_id = b.batch_id
GROUP BY sb.recipe
ORDER BY pct DESC;

-- 4. Room climate summary for yesterday
SELECT r.room_name,
       MIN(c.temp_c) AS min_temp,
       MAX(c.temp_c) AS max_temp,
       AVG(c.humidity) AS avg_humidity,
       MAX(c.co2_ppm) AS peak_co2
FROM climate_readings c
JOIN growing_rooms r ON r.room_id = c.room_id
WHERE CAST(c.read_at AS DATE) = CURRENT_DATE - 1
GROUP BY r.room_name;

-- 5. Top customers by revenue this year, with their favourite species
SELECT c.customer_name,
       c.customer_type,
       SUM(oi.kg * oi.price_per_kg) AS revenue,
       (SELECT oi2.species_name
        FROM order_items oi2
        JOIN orders o2 ON o2.order_id = oi2.order_id
        WHERE o2.customer_id = c.customer_id
        GROUP BY oi2.species_name
        ORDER BY SUM(oi2.kg) DESC
        LIMIT 1) AS favourite_species
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.ordered_at) = EXTRACT(YEAR FROM CURRENT_DATE)
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.customer_name, c.customer_type
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- 6. Open orders that cannot be filled from the last 3 days of harvest
SELECT o.order_id, cu.customer_name, oi.species_name, oi.grade, oi.kg AS ordered_kg,
       COALESCE(SUM(h.weight_kg), 0) AS available_kg
FROM orders o
JOIN customers cu ON cu.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
LEFT JOIN species s ON s.common_name = oi.species_name
LEFT JOIN grow_blocks b ON b.species_id = s.species_id
LEFT JOIN harvests h ON h.block_id = b.block_id
                    AND h.grade = oi.grade
                    AND h.harvested_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '3 days'
WHERE o.status = 'open'
GROUP BY o.order_id, cu.customer_name, oi.species_name, oi.grade, oi.kg
HAVING COALESCE(SUM(h.weight_kg), 0) < oi.kg;

-- 7. Picker productivity: kilograms per picking session day, last 30 days
SELECT h.picker,
       CAST(h.harvested_at AS DATE) AS day,
       SUM(h.weight_kg) AS kg
FROM harvests h
WHERE h.harvested_at >= CURRENT_DATE - 30
  AND h.picker IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY h.picker, CAST(h.harvested_at AS DATE)
ORDER BY day DESC, kg DESC;

-- 8. Blocks due to move to fruiting in the next week
SELECT b.block_id, s.common_name, r.room_name,
       b.inoculated_on + s.colonise_days AS due_to_move
FROM grow_blocks b
JOIN species s ON s.species_id = b.species_id
JOIN growing_rooms r ON r.room_id = b.room_id
WHERE b.moved_to_fruit IS NULL
  AND b.discarded_on IS NULL
  AND b.inoculated_on + s.colonise_days BETWEEN CURRENT_DATE AND CURRENT_DATE + 7
ORDER BY due_to_move;

-- 9. Capacity check: blocks currently in each room against capacity
SELECT r.room_name, r.capacity_blocks, COUNT(b.block_id) AS in_room
FROM growing_rooms r
LEFT JOIN grow_blocks b ON b.room_id = r.room_id AND b.discarded_on IS NULL
WHERE r.active
GROUP BY r.room_id, r.room_name, r.capacity_blocks
HAVING COUNT(b.block_id) > r.capacity_blocks * 0.9;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Stock, deliveries and quality (added last spring)
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE packed_stock (
    stock_id        SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    species_name    TEXT NOT NULL,
    grade           TEXT NOT NULL,
    packed_on       DATE NOT NULL,
    kg              NUMERIC(6,2) NOT NULL,
    use_by          DATE NOT NULL,
    location        TEXT              -- 'chiller 1', 'chiller 2', 'van'
);

CREATE TABLE deliveries (
    delivery_id     SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id        INTEGER REFERENCES orders(order_id),
    driver          TEXT,
    left_at         TIMESTAMP,
    arrived_at      TIMESTAMP,
    temp_on_arrival NUMERIC(3,1),
    rejected_kg     NUMERIC(6,2) DEFAULT 0
);

CREATE TABLE quality_checks (
    check_id        SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    harvest_id      INTEGER REFERENCES harvests(harvest_id),
    checked_on      DATE NOT NULL,
    cap_diameter_mm INTEGER,
    moisture_pct    NUMERIC(4,1),
    passed          BOOLEAN,
    inspector       TEXT,
    comments        TEXT
);

-- 10. Stock that expires within two days, by location
SELECT location, species_name, grade, SUM(kg) AS kg, MIN(use_by) AS earliest
FROM packed_stock
WHERE use_by <= CURRENT_DATE + 2
GROUP BY location, species_name, grade
ORDER BY earliest, location;

-- 11. Late or rejected deliveries by driver, last quarter
SELECT d.driver,
       COUNT(*) AS deliveries,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE d.arrived_at::date > o.delivery_date) AS late,
       SUM(d.rejected_kg) AS rejected_kg,
       AVG(d.temp_on_arrival) AS avg_temp
FROM deliveries d
JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = d.order_id
WHERE EXTRACT(QUARTER FROM d.left_at) = EXTRACT(QUARTER FROM CURRENT_DATE) - 1
GROUP BY d.driver
ORDER BY late DESC;

-- 12. Average days from inoculation to first harvest, per species and room
SELECT s.common_name, r.room_name,
       ROUND(AVG(first_h.first_day - b.inoculated_on), 1) AS avg_days
FROM grow_blocks b
JOIN species s ON s.species_id = b.species_id
JOIN growing_rooms r ON r.room_id = b.room_id
JOIN (SELECT block_id, MIN(CAST(harvested_at AS DATE)) AS first_day
      FROM harvests
      GROUP BY block_id) first_h ON first_h.block_id = b.block_id
GROUP BY s.common_name, r.room_name
ORDER BY s.common_name, avg_days;

-- 13. Blocks whose flush weights are falling: second flush lighter than 40%
--     of the first
SELECT b.block_id, s.common_name,
       f1.weight_kg AS first_flush,
       f2.weight_kg AS second_flush
FROM grow_blocks b
JOIN species s ON s.species_id = b.species_id
JOIN (SELECT block_id, SUM(weight_kg) AS weight_kg
      FROM harvests WHERE flush_number = 1 GROUP BY block_id) f1
  ON f1.block_id = b.block_id
JOIN (SELECT block_id, SUM(weight_kg) AS weight_kg
      FROM harvests WHERE flush_number = 2 GROUP BY block_id) f2
  ON f2.block_id = b.block_id
WHERE f2.weight_kg < f1.weight_kg * 0.4;

-- 14. Monthly revenue and kilograms sold, with the same month last year
SELECT to_char(o.ordered_at, 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
       SUM(oi.kg) AS kg,
       SUM(oi.kg * oi.price_per_kg) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY to_char(o.ordered_at, 'YYYY-MM')
ORDER BY month DESC
LIMIT 24;
```

I wrote this design document for our school's new class booking and attendance system and I'd like it torn apart before we commit money to it. Please give me a proper critique, suggest at least two alternative approaches to the parts you think are weakest, and then draft an implementation plan with phases and the order in which things should be built.

---

# Design: Pirouette, the booking and attendance system for the Aldermere Academy of Dance

Author: Colm Verhoeven (school administrator, with help from the contract developer)
Status: Draft 3, for review
Last updated: 3 October

## 1. Background

The Aldermere Academy of Dance teaches about 640 students between the ages of 3 and 70 across four studios in one building. We run roughly 95 weekly classes in ballet, contemporary, jazz and tap, plus a Saturday pre-professional programme for 41 students aged 11 to 17, a summer school in August, and two stage shows a year (the winter show in December and a spring showcase in May).

Today, booking is a mix of a spreadsheet, a paper register at each studio door, a parent mailing list and a card reader at reception. This causes the problems we all know. Enrolment numbers are wrong because parents email the office, the office updates the spreadsheet days later and teachers are not told. Attendance is on paper, and three times this year a teacher was not told that a child had a medical note. Termly fee invoices take Colm about two full days to produce. Make-up classes for missed lessons are agreed by email and then lost. Costumes for the shows are ordered from a list that is wrong every year.

## 2. Goals

1. Parents can see the timetable, enrol a student in a class, pay termly fees and book make-up classes online.
2. Teachers can mark the register on a tablet at the studio door, see medical notes and emergency contacts, and send a message to the parents of a class.
3. The office can see rolls, waiting lists and balances at any time, and produce the termly invoices in one step.
4. Show administration: casting by class, costume sizes and fees, ticket sales, rehearsal calendar.

## 3. Non-goals

We will not build a general shop, video lessons, a chat system between parents, or a payroll system. Staff payroll stays with the accountant.

## 4. Users and volumes

- 640 students from about 470 families (many have two or three children)
- 22 teachers and accompanists, of whom 14 would mark registers
- 3 office staff
- Peak load: the first day of enrolment each term, when up to 250 families try to book within the first hour at 8:00, which the school announces by email the evening before
- Data volume is small: about 62,000 attendance marks per year

## 5. Proposed architecture

A single web application with a relational database, hosted by a managed platform provider, with a responsive web interface that works on phones and tablets. The parts:

**5.1 Application.** A monolithic server-rendered application written in the contract developer's preferred framework. It exposes pages for parents, teachers and the office. It also exposes a small JSON interface used by the tablet register page so that marks can be saved without reloading.

**5.2 Database.** One PostgreSQL instance with nightly backups kept for 30 days. Tables: families, students, guardians, classes, class_sessions, enrolments, waiting_list, attendance, make_up_bookings, invoices, payments, shows, casting, costumes and notes. The medical notes are stored in a text column on the students table.

**5.3 Payments.** Parents pay by card through an external payment provider's hosted checkout. The application stores only the provider's reference for each payment and never sees card numbers. Termly invoices are created by a monthly job that runs on the 1st and mails a link to the guardian.

**5.4 Email and messages.** Transactional emails (confirmation, invoice, reminders, cancellations) go through an email delivery service. Teachers can send a message to a class, which is sent as email only. No text messages in version 1.

**5.5 Authentication.** Parents sign in with an email address and a one-time code sent by email. Teachers and office staff have a password with no second factor. A family account can have several guardians, each with their own email.

## 6. Key flows

**6.1 Enrolment.** The parent picks a student, then picks a class from those matching the student's age and level. If places are available, the student is enrolled immediately and an invoice line is added. If the class is full the student joins the waiting list. When a place becomes free, the system offers it to the first person on the list by email, who has 48 hours to accept. If they do not respond, the offer passes to the next person.

**6.2 Level changes.** A teacher can move a student up one level. The office confirms the move. There is no automatic check that the target class has space.

**6.3 Attendance.** Before a class, the teacher opens the register on a tablet. The page lists the enrolled students with their photos, any medical notes in red, and a button for present, absent or late. The teacher can add one-off visitors for trial classes. The register is saved after each tap. If the studio network is down, the page keeps the marks in the browser and syncs them when the connection returns.

**6.4 Make-up classes.** If a student is marked absent with notice of at least 24 hours, the family gets one make-up credit, valid for 8 weeks. The parent can use a credit to book into any class at the same or lower level that has an empty place. A student may hold at most three credits.

**6.5 Fees.** The termly fee is calculated as the number of weekly classes times a per-class price, with a sibling discount of 10 percent for the second child and 15 percent for the third and any further children, and a reduction for classes starting after week one. Invoices are due in the second week of term.

**6.6 Show management.** Each show has a cast list per number. Costume fees are added to the next invoice. Ticket sales for the shows are not included in version 1 and will use an outside ticket seller.

**6.7 Cancelled and moved lessons.** If a teacher is ill or a studio is unusable, the office marks the session as cancelled. Every enrolled family receives an email and the session becomes visible as cancelled on the timetable. Each affected student receives a make-up credit automatically, without the 24-hour notice rule. If a whole day is lost, for example because of snow, the office can cancel all sessions for that date in one action. The system does not suggest replacement times, so the office must still agree a new date with the teacher and the studio.

**6.8 Trial classes.** A new family may book one free trial class, limited to one trial per child. The booking takes only a name, a date of birth and an email address and creates a student record with the status "trial". After the class, the teacher marks whether the child would like to join, and the office receives a list each Monday of trial students to contact.

## 7. Privacy and safety

The system holds children's names, photos, medical notes and guardian contacts. Access is limited by role: parents see only their own family; teachers see only students in their own classes; the office sees everything. Photos are used only on the register. Data about former students is deleted after two years unless a family asks us to keep it. We will register the system with the data protection regulator and write a short privacy notice. A teacher's access to a class ends when they are removed from the class. There is no audit log in version 1.

## 8. Hosting and operations

The application will run on a small virtual server with 2 CPUs and 4 gigabytes of memory, costing about 40 pounds per month, plus the database service at about 25 pounds per month. No staging environment is planned; the contract developer will test on a copy of the production data on a laptop. Deployments are by the developer, who will be on call during the first week of each term. Monitoring is limited to an uptime checker that emails Colm.

## 9. Migration

Current data lives in a spreadsheet with one row per student. The developer will write a one-off import script during the summer holiday. Families will be sent an email asking them to check their details on first login. Paper registers continue to be used in parallel for the first term.

## 10. Data model notes

The main tables and their relationships, in short:

- `families` has one row per household, with a billing address and a balance. `guardians` belong to a family and each has an email address, a phone number, and flags for "may collect" and "receives invoices".
- `students` belong to a family and hold date of birth, photo path, level, medical notes and a consent flag for photos at shows.
- `classes` describe the recurring class: name, studio, weekday, start time, length, level, capacity, teacher and price. `class_sessions` are the individual dated lessons generated from a class for the term, so that a cancelled lesson (teacher ill, studio flooded) can be marked on one date only.
- `enrolments` link a student to a class for a term, with a start date and an end date. `attendance` links a student to a class session with a status and the time it was marked.
- `make_up_bookings` link a credit, which is created from an absence, to a class session the student will attend instead.
- `invoices` hold one row per family per term, with lines for classes, costumes and any adjustments. `payments` hold the provider's reference, the amount and the date.

Enrolment capacity is checked in the application: it counts the current enrolments in the class and, if the count is below capacity, inserts a new row. The developer says that at the expected load this is fast enough and that a database lock is not needed. Money amounts are stored as decimal pounds with two places. Dates are stored without time zones because all classes take place in one building.

## 11. Reporting

The office needs five regular reports: the roll by class with medical flags, a list of students with unpaid balances over 30 days, a termly attendance summary per class showing the percentage present, the waiting lists with the date each family joined, and a financial summary of invoiced and received money by month. Reports are produced as pages with a button to download them as a spreadsheet. Teachers need a printable emergency sheet per class, to be kept in a folder at each studio in case the power fails or the network is down.

The director also asked whether the system could show which students have dropped from two classes a week to one, or have missed more than three consecutive lessons, so that the school can phone them before they leave. This is not in the current estimate, but the developer thinks it is a simple query.

## 12. Testing and rollout

The contract developer will write automated tests for the fee calculation and the make-up credit rules, because these are the parts where mistakes cost money and trust. Other parts are tested by hand. Before going live, the office staff will spend two evenings entering a sample of 30 families, including a family with three children, a student with a medical condition, and an adult student. Teachers will try the register at their studios during the December term using test data. There will be a rollback plan only in the sense that paper registers remain available.

Accessibility has not been specified. Several parents and grandparents are older or have limited eyesight, and some use their phones only. The developer has said the interface will use a standard design kit with readable text sizes.

## 13. Cost and timeline

Developer estimate: 38 days of work at 450 pounds per day, or 17,100 pounds, plus hosting for the first year of about 780 pounds, and a payment provider fee of 1.5 percent plus 20 pence per transaction. The aim is to go live for the January term, with the register and fees first and show management after the spring showcase.

| Phase | Content | Estimate |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Students, families, classes, enrolment | 12 days |
| 2 | Register on tablets, notes | 8 days |
| 3 | Fees, invoices, payments | 10 days |
| 4 | Make-up classes, waiting list | 5 days |
| 5 | Show management | 3 days |

## 14. Risks identified so far

- First-day enrolment rush could overload the server.
- Teachers may not accept tablets; two senior teachers have said they prefer paper.
- Studio wireless coverage is poor in studio 3.
- The developer is a single contractor with no backup.

## 15. Open questions

1. Should we offer direct debit instead of card payment? Many families have asked for it.
2. How should part-term enrolment fees be rounded?
3. Do we need to handle adult students differently, since they do not have guardians?
4. Who is allowed to see photos of students?
5. What happens when two guardians in a family disagree, for example over a make-up booking or a level change?

## 16. Alternatives the author considered

Before choosing a custom build, Colm looked at three other routes. The first was a hosted dance-school product from an overseas vendor, priced at about 4 pounds per student per month, or around 30,000 pounds over a year for our numbers. Its register and fee features were good, but it could not handle our sibling discount rule or the make-up credit expiry, and the vendor wanted a two-year contract. The second was to extend the existing spreadsheet with a form for parents and a mail-merge for invoices. This would cost almost nothing but would not fix the register problem or the double-booking of places. The third was a general club-management app used by a neighbouring swimming club, which was cheaper at 9 pounds per month but had no medical note field and no waiting list.

The custom build was chosen because it can match the school's own rules, the school owns the data, and the running cost is low. The main drawback is dependence on one contractor, which is why the source code and a written handover document are listed as deliverables in the draft contract, along with the right for the school to hire another developer to maintain it.
